title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: The night Levin had spent on the haycock did not pass without leaving its mark. The way he had been running his estate revolted him; it had lost all its appeal. In spite of the magnificent harvest, there had never been — or at least it seemed to him there had never been — so many obstacles and so many quarrels between him and the peasants as that year, and the root of these failures and this hostility was now completely clear to him. The pleasure he had taken in the work itself, the closeness with the peasants that grew out of it, the envy he felt for them and their way of life, the desire to live that way — which that night had been not a daydream but a definite intention, the carrying out of which he had worked through in detail — all of it had so changed his view of the farming he had been doing that he could no longer take his old interest in it, and could not help seeing the ugly relation between himself and the workers that lay underneath. The herd of improved cows like Pava, the whole land plowed and enriched, the nine level fields surrounded by hedges, the two hundred and forty acres heavily manured, the seed sown in drills, and all the rest of it — all of it would have been splendid if only the work had been done for themselves, or for themselves and comrades who shared their feelings. But now he saw clearly (his work on a book about agriculture, in which the laborer was to have been the chief element of husbandry, helped him greatly here) that the kind of farming he was carrying on was nothing but a cruel, stubborn struggle between him and his workers, with on one side — his side — a constant intense effort to remake everything along lines he thought better, and on the other side, the natural order of things. And in this struggle, with enormous expenditure of effort on his side and no effort and not even any intention on the other, he saw that all that was achieved was that the work pleased neither side, and that splendid tools, splendid livestock and land were spoiled to no one's benefit. Worst of all, the energy thrown into this work wasn't merely wasted. Now that the meaning of the system had become clear to him, he couldn't help feeling that the very aim of his energy was unworthy. What was the struggle actually about? He was struggling for every farthing of his share (and he had to — relax for a moment, and he wouldn't have had the money to pay his laborers' wages), while they were only struggling to be allowed to do their work easily and pleasantly — that is, as they were used to doing it. It was in his interests for every laborer to work as hard as possible and stay alert, so as not to break the winnowing machines, the horse rakes, the threshing machines, and to pay attention to what he was doing. What the laborer wanted was to work as pleasantly as possible, with rests, and above all carelessly and heedlessly, without thinking. Levin saw this at every step that summer. He sent the men to mow clover for hay, picking out the worst patches where the clover was overgrown with grass and weeds and useless for seed; again and again they mowed the best acres of clover, justifying themselves with the claim that the bailiff had told them to, and trying to reassure him that it would make splendid hay. But he knew they had done it because those acres were so much easier to mow. He sent out a hay machine for pitching the hay — it broke at the first row because it was dull work for a peasant to sit on the seat in front with the great wings waving above him. And he was told, "Don't trouble yourself, your honor — the womenfolk will pitch it quick enough." The plows were practically useless, because it never occurred to the laborer to raise the share when turning the plow; forcing it around, he strained the horses and tore up the ground, and Levin was begged not to mind. The horses were allowed to wander into the wheat because not a single laborer would agree to be night-watchman, and in spite of orders, the laborers insisted on taking turns at night duty, and Ivan, after working all day, fell asleep, and was very repentant about his lapse, saying, "Do what you will with me, your honor."

They killed three of his best calves by letting them into the clover aftermath without watching their drinking, and nothing would convince the men they had been bloated by the clover; they offered him the consolation that one of his neighbors had lost a hundred and twelve head of cattle in three days. None of this happened because anyone bore Levin or his farm ill will; on the contrary, he knew they liked him, considered him a simple gentleman (their highest praise). It happened simply because all they wanted was to work merrily and carelessly, and his interests were not only foreign and incomprehensible to them but in fatal conflict with their most legitimate claims. Levin had long felt dissatisfied with his own position with regard to the land. He saw where his boat was leaking, but he didn't look for the leak — perhaps he was deceiving himself on purpose. (If he lost faith in his work, nothing would be left to him.) But now he could no longer keep up the deception. Farming the land as he had been doing it had become not just unattractive but revolting to him, and he could take no further interest in it.

Added to all this was the presence, only twenty-five miles away, of Kitty Shtcherbatskaya — whom he longed to see and couldn't see. Darya Alexandrovna Oblonskaya had invited him, when he was over there, to come — to come with the aim of renewing his offer to her sister, who, Dolly hinted, would accept him now. Levin himself had felt, on seeing Kitty Shtcherbatskaya, that he had never stopped loving her; but he could not go to the Oblonskys' knowing she was there. The fact that he had made her an offer and she had refused him had set an insurmountable barrier between them. "I can't ask her to be my wife simply because she can't be the wife of the man she wanted to marry," he told himself. The thought made him feel cold and hostile toward her. "I wouldn't be able to talk to her without a feeling of reproach; I couldn't look at her without resentment; and she'll only hate me all the more for it, as she's bound to. And besides — how can I now, after what Darya Alexandrovna told me, go to see them? Can I keep from showing that I know what she told me? And go magnanimously to forgive her, to take pity on her? Put on a show in front of her of forgiving and condescending to grant her my love?... What possessed Darya Alexandrovna to tell me that? By chance I might have seen her, and then everything would have happened of itself; but as it is, it's out of the question — completely out of the question!"
Darya Alexandrovna sent him a letter asking for a side-saddle for Kitty's use. "I'm told you have a side-saddle," she wrote. "I hope you'll bring it over yourself."

This was more than he could bear. How could a woman with any intelligence, any tact, put her sister in such a humiliating position? He wrote ten notes, tore them all up, and sent the saddle without any reply. To write that he would come was impossible, because he could not come; to write that he could not come because something prevented him, or that he would be away, was worse. He sent the saddle without an answer, with a sense of having done something shameful. He handed over the now-revolting business of the estate to the bailiff and set off the next day to a remote district to see his friend Sviazhsky, who had splendid grouse marshes nearby and had recently written to remind him of a long-standing promise to stay with him. The grouse-marsh in the Surovsky district had long tempted Levin, but he had kept putting the trip off because of his work on the estate. Now he was glad to get away from the Shtcherbatskys' neighborhood, and even more from his farm work — especially on a shooting expedition, which in times of trouble had always been the best consolation.

title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: In the Surovsky district there was no railway and no post-horse service, so Levin drove there with his own horses in his big, old-fashioned carriage.

He stopped halfway at a well-off peasant's to feed his horses. A bald, well-preserved old man with a broad red beard going gray on his cheeks opened the gate, squeezing against the gatepost to let the three horses pass. He directed the coachman to a place under the shed in the big, clean, tidy yard with its charred, old-fashioned plows, and asked Levin to come into the parlor. A neatly dressed young woman, with clogs on her bare feet, was scrubbing the floor of the new outer room. She was startled by the dog, who ran in after Levin, and gave a shriek, but burst out laughing at her own fright as soon as she was told the dog wouldn't hurt her. Pointing the way to the parlor door with her bare arm, she bent down again, hiding her handsome face, and went on scrubbing.
"Would you like the samovar?" she asked.
"Yes, please."

The parlor was a big room with a Dutch stove and a screen dividing it in two. Under the holy pictures stood a table painted in patterns, a bench, and two chairs. Near the entrance was a dresser full of crockery. The shutters were closed, there were few flies, and the room was so clean that Levin worried Laska — who had been running along the road and bathing in puddles — would dirty the floor, and ordered her to a corner near the door. After looking around the parlor, Levin went out into the back yard. The good-looking young woman in clogs, swinging the empty pails on her yoke, ran ahead of him to the well for water.

"Look sharp, my girl!" the old man called after her good-humoredly, and he came over to Levin. "So, sir, are you on your way to Nikolay Ivanovitch Sviazhsky? His honor stops by here too," he began, leaning his elbows on the steps' railing and settling in for a chat. In the middle of the old man's account of his acquaintance with Sviazhsky, the gates creaked again, and laborers came into the yard from the fields with wooden plows and harrows. The horses harnessed to them were sleek and fat. The laborers were plainly of the household: two were young men in cotton shirts and caps, and the other two were hired laborers in homespun shirts — one an old man, the other a young fellow. Moving off from the steps, the old man went over to the horses and began unharnessing them.
"What have they been plowing?" Levin asked.
"Plowing up the potatoes. We rent a bit of land too. Fedot, don't let out the gelding — take him to the trough; we'll put the other one in harness."
"Father, the plowshares I ordered — has he brought them?" asked the big, healthy-looking fellow, plainly the old man's son.
"There — in the outer room," the old man answered, gathering up the harness he had taken off and flinging it on the ground. "You can fit them on while they have dinner."

The good-looking young woman came into the outer room with the full pails tugging at her shoulders. More women appeared from somewhere — young and handsome, middle-aged, old and ugly, with children and without.
The samovar began to sing; the laborers and the family, finished with the horses, came in for dinner. Levin got his provisions out of his carriage and invited the old man to take tea with him.
"Well, I've had some today already," said the old man, plainly accepting with pleasure. "But just a glass for company."

Over tea Levin heard all about the old man's farming. Ten years before, the old man had rented three hundred acres from the lady who owned them, and a year ago he had bought them outright and rented another three hundred from a neighboring landowner. A small part — the worst part — he let out for rent, while a hundred acres of arable land he cultivated himself with his family and two hired laborers. The old man complained that things were going badly. But Levin could see he was complaining out of a sense of decorum, and that his farm was in flourishing shape. If it hadn't been, he wouldn't have bought land at thirty-five roubles the acre, wouldn't have married off three sons and a nephew, wouldn't have rebuilt twice after fires — and each time on a larger scale. In spite of the complaints, it was plain that he was proud, and justly proud, of his prosperity, proud of his sons, his nephew, his sons' wives, his horses and cows, and most of all proud of holding the whole operation together. From his conversation with the old man, Levin thought he was not averse to new methods either. He had planted a great many potatoes, and his potatoes — as Levin had seen driving past — were already past flowering and starting to die down, while Levin's were only just coming into flower. He earthed up his potatoes with a modern plow borrowed from a neighboring landowner. He sowed wheat. The small fact that, when thinning his rye, the old man used the rye he thinned out as horse feed especially struck Levin. How many times Levin had seen this splendid fodder wasted and tried to get it saved; but it had always turned out to be impossible. The peasant got it done and couldn't praise it enough as feed for the beasts.
"What have the wenches to do? They carry it out in bundles to the roadside, and the cart brings it away."
"Well, we landowners can't manage well with our laborers," said Levin, passing him a glass of tea.

"Thank you," said the old man, taking the glass but refusing sugar, pointing at a lump he still had. "They're sheer ruin," he said. "Look at Sviazhsky's, for instance. We know what the land's like — first-rate — and yet there's not much of a crop to brag about. It isn't looked after — that's all it comes to!"
"But you work your land with hired laborers?"
"We're all peasants together. We go into everything ourselves. If a man's no use, he can go, and we'll manage on our own."
"Father, Finogen wants some tar," said the young woman in the clogs, coming in.
"Yes, yes, that's how it is, sir!" the old man said, getting up; and crossing himself deliberately, he thanked Levin and went out.

When Levin went into the kitchen to call his coachman, he saw the whole family at dinner. The women were standing up waiting on them. The young, sturdy-looking son was telling some funny story with his mouth full of pudding, and they were all laughing — the woman in the clogs, ladling cabbage soup into a bowl, laughing the most merrily of all.

Very likely the good-looking face of the young woman in clogs had a great deal to do with the sense of well-being this peasant household gave Levin, but the impression was so strong that Levin couldn't shake it off. All the way from the old peasant's to Sviazhsky's he kept turning back to this peasant farm, as though there were something in the impression that demanded special attention from him.

title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: Sviazhsky was the marshal of his district. He was five years older than Levin, and had been married a long while. His sister-in-law, a young woman Levin liked very much, lived with them, and Levin knew Sviazhsky and his wife would have been delighted to see her married off to him. He knew it with the certainty that so-called eligible young men always know such things, even if he could never have brought himself to mention it to anyone; and he knew too that, although he wanted to marry, and although by every measure this very attractive girl would make an excellent wife, he could no more have married her, even setting aside his love for Kitty Shtcherbatskaya, than he could have flown to the moon. And that knowledge poisoned the pleasure he had hoped to find in the visit.

When Sviazhsky's letter arrived with the shooting invitation, Levin had thought of all this at once; but even so he had decided that Sviazhsky's matchmaking ambitions for him were only his own groundless guess, and that he would go anyway. And, at the bottom of his heart, he wanted to test himself in regard to this girl. The Sviazhskys' home life was exceptionally pleasant, and Sviazhsky himself, the best example Levin knew of a man involved in local public affairs, was very interesting to him.

Sviazhsky was one of those people who never stopped puzzling Levin — people whose convictions, perfectly logical though never original, run along one track on their own, while their actual life, very definite and firm in its direction, runs along another track entirely and almost always in direct contradiction. Sviazhsky was an extremely progressive man. He looked down on the nobility, believed that most of his fellow nobles secretly favored serfdom and were only hiding it out of cowardice, and regarded Russia as a ruined country, somewhere along the lines of Turkey, with a government so bad he never permitted himself to criticize its actions seriously — and yet he was a functionary of that government, a model marshal of the nobility, and whenever he drove out he wore the official cockade and the cap with the red band. He considered human life only tolerable abroad, and he went abroad at every chance — while at the same time running an elaborate, improved farming operation in Russia and following with the keenest interest everything happening in the country. He believed the Russian peasant occupied an evolutionary stage somewhere between ape and man, and yet in the local assemblies no one was quicker to shake hands with peasants and listen to their views. He believed neither in God nor the devil, but he worried a great deal about improving the clergy and maintaining their income, and he made a special effort to keep the village church in good repair.

On the woman question he was firmly with the radicals — full liberty for women, especially the right to work. And yet he and his wife lived together on such terms that their affectionate, childless household was the envy of everyone, and he arranged his wife's days so that she did nothing, and could do nothing, except share in his efforts to fill her time as happily and agreeably as possible.

If it hadn't been part of Levin's nature to put the kindest interpretation on people, Sviazhsky's character would have presented no puzzle at all: he would simply have said to himself, "a fool or a knave," and everything would have been clear. But he couldn't say "fool," because Sviazhsky was unmistakably intelligent — and, more than that, a highly cultivated man who was unusually modest about his culture. There was no subject he knew nothing about. But he didn't put his knowledge on display unless he had to. Still less could Levin call him a knave, since he was plainly an honest, kindhearted, sensible man who went about his work with good humor, sharp focus, and persistence; he was held in high regard by everyone around him, and he had certainly never knowingly done — and was indeed incapable of doing — anything base.
Levin tried to make sense of him and couldn't, and so he looked at him and his life as at a living enigma.

He and Sviazhsky were on friendly terms, and so Levin used to test him, trying to get down to the very foundation of his view of life; but it was always useless. Every time Levin tried to push past the outer chambers of Sviazhsky's mind — chambers hospitably open to anyone — he saw Sviazhsky grow faintly uncomfortable; a flicker of alarm would show in his eyes, as though he were afraid Levin would understand him, and he would give Levin a kindly, good-natured rebuff.

Just now, in his disillusionment with farming, Levin was especially glad to stay with Sviazhsky. Apart from the fact that the sight of this happy, affectionate couple, so satisfied with themselves and with everyone else, and their well-run household, always lifted his spirits, he felt a longing — now that he was so dissatisfied with his own life — to get at whatever secret Sviazhsky had that gave him such clarity, definiteness, and good courage in living. Beyond that, Levin knew that at Sviazhsky's he would meet the local landowners, and right now he was particularly eager to hear and join in those country conversations about crops, wages, and the rest — talk that, he was aware, is conventionally dismissed as something very low, but which seemed to him at the moment to be the one subject that mattered. "Maybe it wasn't important in the days of serfdom, and maybe it isn't important in England. In both cases the conditions of agriculture have been firmly settled; but with us, now that everything has been turned upside down and is only just beginning to take shape, the question of what form these conditions will take is the only question that matters in Russia," Levin thought.

The shooting turned out worse than Levin had expected. The marsh was dry and there were no grouse to speak of. He walked all day and came back with only three birds, but he brought back, as he always did from a day in the field, an excellent appetite, excellent spirits, and the kind of sharp, intellectual mood that with him always followed hard physical exertion. And out in the marsh, when he seemed to be thinking of nothing in particular, the old peasant and his family kept coming back to him, and the impression they had left seemed to demand not just his attention but the resolution of some question tied up with them.
In the evening, at tea, two landowners had come on some business about a wardship and joined the party, and the kind of conversation Levin had been hoping for started up.

Levin was sitting beside his hostess at the tea table, and he had to keep up some sort of conversation with her and with her sister, who was across from him. Madame Sviazhskaya was a round-faced, fair-haired, rather short woman, all smiles and dimples. Levin tried to use her to get at the formidable puzzle her husband presented to him; but his thoughts weren't entirely free, because he was in agonies of embarrassment. The cause was the sister-in-law, sitting directly across from him in a dress — put on, he imagined, specifically for his benefit — cut particularly low, trapeze-shaped, over her white bosom. That quadrangular opening, despite the bosom being very white — or precisely because it was so very white — robbed Levin of the full use of his wits. He imagined, probably wrongly, that the low-cut bodice had been made on his account, and he felt he had no right to look at it, and tried not to look at it; but he also felt that he was somehow to blame for its having been made in the first place. It seemed to him that he had deceived someone, that he owed someone an explanation, that no such explanation was possible — and for that reason he kept blushing, fidgeting, and saying the wrong thing. His awkwardness rubbed off on the pretty sister-in-law too. But their hostess seemed not to notice, and kept deliberately drawing her into the conversation.

"You say," she was saying, picking up the subject they had started on, "that my husband can't be interested in anything Russian. On the contrary — he's always in cheerful spirits abroad, but not the way he is here. Here he feels in his proper place. He has so much to do, and he has a knack for taking an interest in everything. Oh — you haven't been to see our school, have you?"
"I have seen it... The little house covered in ivy, isn't it?"
"Yes; that's Nastia's work," she said, nodding toward her sister.
"Do you teach there yourself?" Levin asked, trying to look above the low neckline but feeling that wherever he looked in that direction he would see it.
"Yes; I used to teach there myself, and I still do, but we have a first-rate schoolmistress now. And we've added gymnastic exercises."

"No, thank you, no more tea for me," Levin said, and, knowing he was being rude but unable to keep up the conversation, he stood up, blushing. "I hear an interesting conversation," he added, and walked off to the other end of the table, where Sviazhsky was sitting with the two country gentlemen. Sviazhsky was sitting sideways, one elbow on the table, a cup in one hand, while with the other he was gathering up his beard, holding it to his nose, then letting it fall again, as though he were smelling it. His brilliant black eyes were fixed on the excited country gentleman with gray whiskers, and he was apparently enjoying the man's remarks. The gentleman was complaining about the peasants. It was clear to Levin that Sviazhsky had a ready answer that would have demolished the man's whole position, but that he couldn't deliver it from where he stood, and was instead listening, not without pleasure, to the landowner's comic tirade.

The gentleman with the gray whiskers was plainly an unrepentant defender of serfdom and a devoted farmer who had spent his whole life in the country. Levin saw the proof in his clothes — the old-fashioned, threadbare coat that was obviously not his everyday wear — in his shrewd, deep-set eyes, in his idiomatic, fluent Russian, in the commanding tone that long use had made habitual, and in the firm gestures of his large, red, sun-darkened hands, with an old betrothal ring on the little finger.

title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: "If I'd only the heart to give up what's been set in motion... so much trouble wasted... I'd turn my back on the whole thing, sell up, go off like Nikolay Ivanovitch... to hear _La Belle Hélène_," said the landowner, a pleasant smile lighting up his shrewd old face.
"But you don't give it up," said Nikolay Ivanovitch Sviazhsky; "so there must be something in it for you."

"The only thing in it for me is that I live in my own house — neither bought nor rented. Beyond that, one keeps hoping the people will come to their senses. Though it's the other way round — you wouldn't believe the drunkenness, the immorality! They keep cutting up their bits of land and swapping them around. Not a sight of a horse or a cow anywhere. The peasant is dying of hunger, but just try taking him on as a hired hand — he'll do his best to spite you, and then haul you up before the justice of the peace."
"But you go to the justice yourself," Sviazhsky said.

"Lodge complaints? Not for anything in the world! Such talk and such a fuss — you'd be sorry you ever started. Take the works — they pocketed the advance and ran off. What did the justice do? Acquitted them. Nothing keeps them in line but their own village court and their village elder. He'll flog them the old-fashioned way! Take that away and there's nothing left but to throw it all up and run."
Plainly the landowner was teasing Sviazhsky, who, far from taking offense, seemed to be enjoying it.
"But we run our places without anything that extreme," he said, smiling. "Levin and I — and this gentleman."
He indicated the other landowner.
"Yes, the thing's being done at Mihail Petrovitch's — but ask him how. Do you call that a rational system?" said the landowner, obviously rather pleased with the word "rational."

"My system is very simple," said Mihail Petrovitch. "Thank God. My whole management comes down to having the money ready for the autumn taxes, and the peasants come to me — 'Father, master, help us!' Well, they're all one's neighbors; one feels for them. So one fronts them a third, but one says, 'Remember, lads — I have helped you, and you must help me when I need it — whether it's the sowing of the oats, or the haymaking, or the harvest'; and they agree, so much for each taxpayer — though some of them are dishonest, that's true."
Levin, who had long been familiar with these patriarchal arrangements, exchanged a look with Sviazhsky and cut Mihail Petrovitch off, turning back to the gentleman with the gray whiskers.
"Then what do you think?" he asked. "What sort of system should one go with nowadays?"

"Manage the way Mihail Petrovitch does — or rent the land out for half the crop or for cash to the peasants. You can do that — only that's exactly how the general prosperity of the country is being destroyed. Where the land used to yield nine to one with serf labor and proper management, on the half-crop system it yields three to one. Russia has been ruined by the emancipation!"

Sviazhsky looked at Levin with smiling eyes and even made a small ironic gesture at him; but Levin didn't find the landowner's words ridiculous — he understood them better than he understood Sviazhsky. A good deal more of what the gentleman with the gray whiskers said in support of his view that Russia had been ruined by the emancipation struck Levin as quite true, new to him, and impossible to argue against. The landowner was plainly voicing his own thought — something that happens very rarely — and a thought he hadn't arrived at out of a need to exercise an idle mind, but one that had grown up out of the conditions of his life, that he had brooded over in the solitude of his village and considered from every angle.

"The point, you see, is that progress of any kind only happens through the exercise of authority," he said, plainly wanting to show that he was not without culture. "Take the reforms of Peter, of Catherine, of Alexander. Take European history. And progress in agriculture more than anywhere else — the potato, for instance, was introduced among us by force. The wooden plough wasn't always used either. It was probably brought in sometime before the Empire, but it was brought in by force. Now, in our own time, we landowners under serfdom introduced all sorts of improvements: drying machines, threshing machines, the cartage of manure, all the modern implements — we brought all of it in on our own authority, and the peasants opposed it at first, and then ended up imitating us. Now, with the abolition of serfdom, our authority has been taken away; and so our farming, where it had been raised to a high level, is bound to sink back to the most primitive, savage condition. That's how I see it."
"But why? If it's rational, you'll be able to maintain the same system with hired labor," Sviazhsky said.
"We have no power over them. With whom, may I ask, am I going to run the system?"
"There it is — the labor force — the central element of agriculture," Levin thought.
"With laborers."

"The laborers won't work properly, and won't work with good implements. Our laborer can do nothing but get drunk like a pig, and once he's drunk he ruins whatever you give him. He makes the horses sick on too much water, he cuts good harness, he barters the wheel tires for drink, he drops bits of iron into the threshing machine just to break it. He hates the sight of anything that isn't done in his usual way. And that's how the level of farming has dropped everywhere. Lands gone out of cultivation, overgrown with weeds, or carved up among the peasants, and where millions of bushels used to be raised you get a hundred thousand; the wealth of the country has gone down. If the same thing had been done, but with proper care..."
And he went on to lay out his own scheme of emancipation, which, in his view, would have avoided all these drawbacks.
This didn't interest Levin, but when the landowner was done, Levin went back to his earlier point and, turning to Sviazhsky, tried to draw out a serious opinion from him.

"That the standard of farming is dropping, and that under our current relationship to the peasants there is no possibility of running an operation on a rational system that turns a profit — that's perfectly true," he said.

"I don't believe it," Sviazhsky answered, quite seriously. "All I see is that we don't know how to cultivate the land, and that our farming under serfdom was not too advanced, but actually too primitive. We have no machinery, no good stock, no proper supervision; we don't even know how to keep accounts. Ask any landowner — he can't tell you which crop is profitable and which isn't."
"Italian bookkeeping," said the gentleman with the gray whiskers ironically. "You can keep your books however you like, but if they ruin everything for you, there'll be no profit anyway."

"Why do they ruin things? They'll break a poor threshing machine, or your Russian press — but they don't break my steam press. They'll ruin a wretched Russian nag — but give them good dray horses and the dray horses are fine. It's the same all the way around. We have to lift our farming to a higher level."
"Oh, if only one had the means, Nikolay Ivanovitch! It's easy enough for you; but for me, with a son at the university and boys at the high school — how am I going to buy dray horses?"
"That's what the land banks are for."
"So that what I have left can be auctioned off? No, thank you."

"I don't agree that it's necessary or even possible to raise the level of agriculture any further," Levin said. "I throw myself into it, I have means, and I can do nothing. As for the banks — I don't know who they actually help. For my part, anyway, whatever I've spent money on in the way of farming, it's been a loss: livestock — a loss, machinery — a loss."
"That's true enough," the gentleman with the gray whiskers chimed in, positively laughing with satisfaction.

"And I'm not the only one," Levin went on. "I see all the neighboring landowners who are working their land on a rational system; almost without exception they're doing it at a loss. Come, tell us — does your land pay?" Levin asked, and at once he caught in Sviazhsky's eyes that fleeting expression of alarm he had noticed every time he tried to push past the outer chambers of Sviazhsky's mind.

Besides, the question wasn't entirely fair on Levin's part. Madame Sviazhskaya had told him at tea that they had brought in a German bookkeeping expert from Moscow that summer, who, for a fee of five hundred roubles, had gone through the management of their estate and concluded that they were running a loss of just over three thousand roubles. She didn't remember the precise figure, but apparently the German had worked it out to a fraction of a kopeck.
The gray-whiskered landowner smiled at the mention of Sviazhsky's farming profits, plainly aware just how much his neighbor and marshal was likely to be making.
"Possibly it doesn't pay," Sviazhsky answered. "That only proves that either I'm a bad manager, or that I've sunk my capital into raising the rent value of my land."

"Oh, rent!" Levin cried in dismay. "Rent there may be in Europe, where the land has been improved by the labor put into it — but with us all the land is being run down by the labor put into it. In other words they're working it out. So there's no question of rent."
"What do you mean, no rent? It's a law."
"Then we're outside the law; rent doesn't explain anything for us, it just confuses things. No, tell me how there can be a theory of rent —"
"Would you like some junket? Masha, pass us some junket or raspberries." He turned to his wife. "The raspberries are lasting unusually late this year."
And in the most cheerful mood, Sviazhsky got up and walked off, apparently assuming the conversation was over at the very moment Levin felt it was just beginning.

Having lost his sparring partner, Levin went on with the gray-whiskered landowner, trying to convince him that the whole difficulty came from the fact that we don't bother to learn the peculiarities and habits of our laborer; but the landowner, like everyone who thinks independently and in isolation, was slow to absorb anyone else's idea and especially partial to his own. He stuck to his view that the Russian peasant was a swine and liked his swinishness, and that to get him out of it one had to have authority — and there was none — one had to have the stick, and we had become so liberal that we had suddenly replaced the stick that had served us for a thousand years with lawyers and model prisons, where the worthless, stinking peasant was fed good soup and given a fixed allowance of cubic feet of air.
"What makes you think," Levin said, trying to steer back to the question, "that it's impossible to find some relationship to the laborer in which the labor would actually become productive?"
"That could never happen with the Russian peasantry; we have no power over them," the landowner answered.

"How can new conditions be found?" Sviazhsky said. He had eaten some junket and lit a cigarette, and now he came back to the discussion. "Every possible relationship to the labor force has been defined and studied," he said. "The relic of barbarism — the primitive commune with each guaranteeing for all — will disappear on its own; serfdom has been abolished; what's left is free labor, and its forms have been fixed and worked out already, and have to be adopted. Permanent hands, day-laborers, rammers — you can't get outside those forms."
"But Europe is dissatisfied with those forms."
"Dissatisfied, and looking for new ones. And will find them, in all likelihood."
"That's exactly what I was getting at," Levin answered. "Why shouldn't we look for them ourselves?"
"Because that would be like reinventing the way to build a railway. They're already there, already invented."
"But what if they don't fit us? What if they're stupid?" Levin said.
And again he caught the look of alarm in Sviazhsky's eyes.

"Oh, yes — we'll throw our caps over the windmill! We've found the secret Europe was looking for! I've heard it all before; but, forgive me — do you know everything that's been done in Europe on the question of organizing labor?"
"No, very little."

"It's the question absorbing the best minds in Europe right now. The Schulze-Delitsch movement... And then the enormous literature on the labor question — the most liberal Lassalle movement... the Mulhausen experiment? That's a fact by now, as you're no doubt aware."
"I have some idea of it, but only vaguely."
"No, you only say that; you must know about it as well as I do. I'm no professor of sociology, of course, but it interested me, and honestly, if it interests you, you really ought to study it."
"But what conclusion have they reached?"
"Excuse me..."
The two neighbors had stood up, and Sviazhsky, once again heading off Levin's awkward habit of peeking past the outer chambers of his mind, went to see his guests out.

title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: Levin was insufferably bored that evening with the ladies; he had been stirred as never before by the thought that the dissatisfaction he was feeling with his way of running his estate wasn't a one-off case, but the general state of things in Russia — that working out some relationship between laborers and the soil where they would actually work, as with the peasant he had met on the road to the Sviazhskys', was not a dream but a problem that had to be solved. And it seemed to him the problem could be solved — and that he was the one who ought to try to solve it.

After saying good night to the ladies and promising to stay through the next day so as to ride out with them to see an interesting ruin in the crown forest, Levin went, before turning in, into his host's study to pick up the books on the labor question that Sviazhsky had offered him. Sviazhsky's study was a huge room, walled in by bookcases, with two tables — one a heavy writing-table set in the middle of the room, the other a round table covered with the latest issues of reviews and journals in various languages, arranged like the rays of a star around the lamp. On the writing-table stood a set of drawers labeled in gold lettering and stuffed with papers of every sort.
Sviazhsky pulled out the books and dropped into a rocking chair.
"What are you looking at there?" he said to Levin, who was standing at the round table flipping through the reviews.

"Oh, yes — there's a very interesting article in there," Sviazhsky said of the review Levin was holding. "It seems," he went on with eager interest, "that Friedrich wasn't actually the one chiefly responsible for the partition of Poland. It's been proved..."

And with his usual clarity, he summed up the new, very important, very interesting revelations. Even though Levin was absorbed at that moment by his ideas about the land, he wondered, as he listened to Sviazhsky: "What is there inside this man? And why, of all things, is he interested in the partition of Poland?" When Sviazhsky had finished, Levin couldn't help asking, "Well — and so what?" But there was no "so what." It was simply interesting that things had been shown to be such and such. And Sviazhsky offered no explanation, and saw no need to explain why it was interesting to him.
"Yes — but I was very interested by your irritable neighbor," Levin said with a sigh. "He's a sharp fellow, and a lot of what he said was true."
"Oh, come on! An incurable defender of serfdom at heart, like all of them!" Sviazhsky said.
"Whose marshal you happen to be."
"Yes — only I marshal them in the opposite direction," Sviazhsky said, laughing.

"Here's what really interests me," Levin said. "He's right that our system — rational farming — doesn't answer, and the only thing that does answer is the money-lender approach, like the meek-looking gentleman's, or the simplest possible setup... Whose fault is it?"
"Ours, of course. Besides, it isn't true that it doesn't answer. It answers with Vassiltchikov."
"A factory..."

"But really I don't know what surprises you. The people are at such a low stage of rational and moral development that obviously they're bound to resist anything that's foreign to them. In Europe, a rational system works because the people are educated; therefore we must educate our people — that's all."
"But how do we educate the people?"
"To educate the people, three things are needed: schools, and schools, and schools."
"But you said yourself that the people are at such a low stage of material development — what good will schools do for that?"

"You know, you remind me of the story about the advice given to the sick man — try a purgative. Tried it: worse. Try leeches. Tried them: worse. Well, then, nothing left but prayer. Tried it: worse. That's just how it is with us. I say political economy; you say — worse. I say socialism: worse. Education: worse."
"But how do schools help?"
"They give the peasant new wants."

"Well, that's something I've never understood," Levin shot back. "In what way are schools going to help the people improve their material position? You say schools and education will give them new wants. So much the worse — since they won't be in any position to satisfy them. And how knowing addition and subtraction and the catechism is going to improve their material condition, I've never been able to work out. The other evening I met a peasant woman with a little baby and asked her where she was going. She said she was going to the wise woman; her boy had screaming fits, so she was taking him to be treated. I asked, 'Well, and how does the wise woman cure screaming fits?' 'She puts the child on the hen-roost and says a charm over him...'"
"There — you're saying it yourself! What's needed to keep her from taking her child to the hen-roost to cure his screaming fits is exactly..." Sviazhsky said, smiling good-humoredly.

"Oh, no!" Levin said, irritated. "That cure was just a comparison — for the cure of treating the people with schools. The people are poor and ignorant — we see that as surely as the peasant woman sees that her baby is ill, because it's screaming. But how this trouble of poverty and ignorance is going to be cured by schools is as incomprehensible as how the hen-roost cures the screaming. What has to be cured is whatever is making him poor."

"Well, on that point at least you're in agreement with Spencer — whom you so dislike. He says the same thing — that education may follow from greater prosperity and comfort, from more frequent washing, as he puts it, but not from being able to read and write..."

"Well, then, I'm very glad — or rather very sorry — to be in agreement with Spencer; but I've known it a long time. Schools can do no good; what will do good is an economic arrangement in which the people become wealthier, get more leisure — and then there will be schools."
"Still, all over Europe schools are obligatory now."
"And how far do you yourself agree with Spencer on the question?" Levin asked.
But there was a glint of alarm in Sviazhsky's eyes, and he smiled and said:
"No — that screaming story is positively priceless! Did you really hear it yourself?"

Levin saw he was never going to find the connection between this man's life and his ideas. Plainly he didn't care in the least what his line of reasoning led him to; all he wanted was the process of reasoning itself. And he didn't like it when that process backed him into a corner. That was the one thing he disliked, and he steered around it by switching the conversation to something pleasant and entertaining.

All the impressions of the day — starting with the impression made by the old peasant, which served as a sort of foundation for everything else — threw Levin into violent excitement. This dear, decent Sviazhsky, keeping a stock of ideas in reserve for purely social uses, plainly having some other principles hidden away from Levin, while with the crowd, whose name is legion, he was shaping public opinion with ideas he didn't himself share; that hot-tempered country gentleman, perfectly correct in the conclusions life had hammered into him, but wrong in his bitterness against a whole class — and the best class in Russia at that; his own dissatisfaction with the work he had been doing, and the vague hope of finding a remedy for all of it — all of it blended into a sense of inward churning and an anticipation of some solution very close at hand.

Left alone in the room they had given him, lying on a spring mattress that yielded unexpectedly under every movement of his arm or leg, Levin couldn't fall asleep for a long while. Not a single one of Sviazhsky's lines, however clever, had really interested him; but the irascible landowner's conclusions deserved a careful look. Levin couldn't help running back over every word the man had said, and revising in his head his own replies.

"Yes, what I should have said to him was — you say our farming doesn't work because the peasant hates improvements, and they have to be forced on him from above. If no system of farming worked at all without those improvements, you'd be entirely right. But the one system that does work is the one where the laborer is working in accordance with his own habits, just like the old peasant's land on the way here. Your dissatisfaction and ours with the existing system shows that either we are to blame or the laborers are. We've gone on our way — the European way — for a long time without ever asking ourselves about the qualities of our labor force. Let's try looking at the labor force not as some abstract force but as the _Russian peasant_ with his own instincts, and we'll arrange our farming accordingly. Imagine, I ought to have said to him, that you have the same setup the old peasant has, that you've found a way to make your laborers take an interest in the success of the work, and that you've found a happy middle ground in the kind of improvements they'll accept — and you'll get, without exhausting the soil, two or three times the yield you got before. Divide it in halves, give half as the laborers' share; the surplus left to you will be greater, and the laborers' share will be greater too. And to make this work, one has to lower the standard of farming and get the laborers interested in its success. How to do that? — that's a matter of detail; but it can be done, no doubt about it."

The idea threw Levin into a great state of excitement. He didn't sleep half the night, working out in detail how to put the idea into practice. He hadn't planned to leave the next day, but now he was determined to head home early in the morning. Besides, the sister-in-law with her low-cut bodice stirred in him a feeling close to shame and remorse, as though he had committed some thoroughly base act. Most important of all — he had to get back without delay: he would have to hurry to put his new plan to the peasants before the sowing of the winter wheat, so that the sowing could be done on the new footing. He had made up his mind to overhaul his whole system.

title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: Carrying out Levin's plan ran into many obstacles, but he kept at it, putting in every effort, and reached a result that, while not what he had hoped for, was enough to let him believe — without lying to himself — that the attempt had been worth the trouble. One of the chief obstacles was that the work of cultivating the land was already in full swing; it was impossible to stop everything and start over from scratch, and the machine had to be repaired while it was still running.

On the evening he got home, when he laid out his plan for the bailiff, the bailiff, with visible pleasure, agreed with everything Levin said — for as long as Levin was pointing out that all the work done up to then had been stupid and useless. The bailiff said he had been saying so for years, but nobody had listened to him. As for Levin's actual proposal — that he take a share alongside his laborers in each agricultural venture — at that the bailiff simply expressed deep gloom, offered no clear opinion, and immediately started talking about the urgent need to cart in the rest of the rye sheaves the next day and to send the men out for the second ploughing, so that Levin felt this was no time to argue it through.

When he began talking to the peasants about it, and proposing to hand the land over to them on new terms, he ran into the same enormous obstacle: they were so absorbed in the day's work that they had no time to weigh the advantages or disadvantages of the scheme.

Simple-hearted Ivan, the cowherd, seemed to grasp Levin's proposal completely — that he and his family take a share of the profits from the cattle yard — and he was fully on board with the plan. But when Levin started in on the future advantages, Ivan's face filled with alarm and regret that he could not stay to hear the rest, and he hurried off to find himself some chore that wouldn't wait: he either grabbed a pitchfork to throw hay out of the pens, or rushed off to fetch water or muck out the dung.

Another obstacle was the peasants' unshakable conviction that a landowner could not possibly have any motive other than wanting to squeeze as much as he could out of them. They were firmly persuaded that his real goal (whatever he might say to them) would always lie in what he didn't say. And they themselves, when giving their views, said a great deal but never the actual point. On top of that (Levin felt the irascible landowner had been right about this) the peasants made it their first and unalterable condition of any deal whatsoever that they would not be forced to use any new method of tillage or any new implements. They agreed that the modern plough plowed better, that the scarifier did the work faster, but they came up with a thousand reasons why neither was actually usable for them. And though Levin had accepted the necessity of lowering the standard of cultivation, he was sorry to give up improved methods whose advantages were so plain. But despite all this he got his way, and by autumn the system was working — or at least so it seemed to him.

At first Levin had thought of handing over the running of the whole farm just as it was to the peasants, the laborers, and the bailiff under new partnership terms; but he quickly saw that was impossible, and decided to divide it up. The cattle yard, the kitchen garden, the hay fields, and the arable land, broken into several parts, had to be turned into separate lots. The simple-hearted cowherd Ivan, who, Levin thought, understood the whole thing better than anyone, gathered a working gang — mostly from his own family — and became a partner in the cattle yard. A distant part of the estate, a tract of waste land that had lain fallow for eight years, was taken on with the help of the clever carpenter Fyodor Ryezunov by six peasant families on the new partnership terms, and the peasant Shuraev took over the running of all the kitchen gardens on the same terms. The rest of the land was still worked on the old system, but these three associated partnerships were the first step toward a new arrangement for the whole, and they took up all of Levin's time.

It's true that in the cattle yard things went no better than before, and Ivan strenuously opposed warm housing for the cows and butter made from fresh cream, insisting that cows need less feed when kept cold, and that butter from sour cream is more profitable, and he asked for wages just as under the old system, taking not the slightest interest in the fact that the money he was receiving wasn't wages but an advance against his future share of the profits.

It's true that Fyodor Ryezunov's company did not plow the ground twice before sowing, as had been agreed, defending themselves on the grounds that the time was too short. It's true that the peasants in the same company, though they had agreed to work the land on the new terms, always spoke of the land not as held in partnership but as rented for half the crop, and more than once both the peasants and Ryezunov himself said to Levin, "If you'd just take rent for the land, it would save you the trouble, and we'd be more free." And the same peasants kept postponing, on various excuses, the building of a cattle yard and a barn on the land as agreed, dragging it out until winter.

It's true that Shuraev would have liked to sublet the kitchen gardens he had taken on in small plots to the peasants. He plainly didn't understand — and apparently deliberately didn't understand — the terms on which the land had been given to him.

Often, too, when Levin talked with the peasants and laid out all the advantages of the plan for them, he could feel that they were hearing only the sound of his voice, and were firmly resolved, no matter what he said, not to be taken in. He felt this especially when he spoke to the cleverest of them, Ryezunov, and caught the glint in Ryezunov's eyes that gave away both ironic amusement at Levin and the firm conviction that, if anyone was going to be taken in, it wasn't going to be him, Ryezunov. But in spite of all this Levin thought the system was working, and that by keeping strict accounts and insisting on his own way, he would in time prove to them the advantages of the arrangement — and then the system would carry itself.

These matters, together with the running of the land still in his own hands and his indoor work on the book, kept Levin so busy the whole summer that he barely ever went out shooting. At the end of August he heard from the servant who brought back the side-saddle that the Oblonskys had gone away to Moscow. He felt that by not answering Darya Alexandrovna's letter, in a piece of rudeness he could not think back on without burning, he had burned his ships, and he would never go to see them again. He had been just as rude with the Sviazhskys, leaving them without saying goodbye. But he would never go to see them again either. It didn't matter to him now. The business of reorganizing his farm absorbed him so completely it was as if there would never be anything else in his life. He read through the books Sviazhsky had lent him, and, copying out what he didn't yet have, he read both the political economy and the socialist books on the question, but, as he had expected, he found nothing that touched the scheme he had undertaken. In the books on political economy — Mill, for instance, whom he plowed through first with great eagerness, hoping at every page for an answer to the questions taking him over — he found laws drawn from the conditions of European agriculture; but he couldn't see why those laws, which didn't apply in Russia, should be universal. He saw the same thing in the socialist books: either they were the lovely but impossible fantasies that had fascinated him as a student, or they were attempts to patch up, to correct, the economic situation Europe was in, with which the system of land tenure in Russia had nothing in common. Political economy told him that the laws by which Europe's wealth had developed, and was still developing, were universal and constant. Socialism told him that development along those lines led straight to ruin. And neither one gave him an answer, or even a hint of one, in reply to the question of what he, Levin, and all the Russian peasants and landowners, were supposed to do with their millions of hands and millions of acres to make them as productive as possible for the common good.

Having once taken up the subject, he conscientiously read everything bearing on it, and meant to go abroad in the autumn to study land systems on the spot, so that he wouldn't be ambushed on this question the way he had so often been on others. So often, just as he was starting to understand the idea of someone he was talking to and was starting to explain his own, he would suddenly be told: "But Kauffmann? But Jones? But Dubois? But Michelli? You haven't read them — they've worked the question out completely."

He saw clearly now that Kauffmann and Michelli had nothing to tell him. He knew what he wanted. He saw that Russia had splendid land and splendid laborers, and that in certain cases — as with the peasant on the way to Sviazhsky's — the output of the laborers and the land was great; but that in the majority of cases, when capital was applied in the European way, the output was small, and this was simply because the laborers were willing to work, and to work well, only in their own peculiar way, and this antagonism was not accidental but constant, and rooted in the national spirit. He thought that the Russian people, whose task it was to colonize and cultivate vast tracts of unoccupied land, had consciously, until all their land was occupied, stuck to the methods suited to that task, and that those methods were nowhere near as bad as people generally believed. And he wanted to prove this theoretically in his book and practically on his own land.

title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: By the end of September the timber had been carted in for the cattle yard on the land allotted to the peasants' association, and the butter from the cows had been sold and the profits divided. In practice the system was working splendidly — or at least so it seemed to Levin. To work the subject out theoretically and finish his book — which in Levin's daydreams was not just going to revolutionize political economy but to demolish that science entirely and lay the foundation for a new science of the relationship between the people and the soil — all that was left was to take a tour abroad, study on the spot whatever had been done along the same lines, and gather conclusive evidence that what had been done there was not what was needed. Levin was just waiting on the delivery of his wheat to receive the money for it and set off. But then the rains began, preventing the harvest of the corn and potatoes left in the fields, and putting a stop to all the work, even to the delivery of the wheat.
The mud on the roads was impassable; two mills were carried off, and the weather kept getting worse.

On the 30th of September the sun came out in the morning, and, hoping for fine weather, Levin began making his final preparations to set off. He gave orders for the wheat to be delivered, sent the bailiff to the merchant to collect the money owed him, and went out himself to give a few last directions on the estate before leaving.

Having finished his business, soaked through by the streams of water running down the leather behind his neck and into his gaiters, but in the sharpest and most confident of moods, Levin rode home in the evening. The weather had grown worse than ever toward evening; the hail lashed his drenched mare so hard that she went along sideways, shaking her head and ears; but Levin was fine under his hood, and looked out cheerfully at the muddy streams running under the wheels, at the drops hanging from every bare twig, at the patch of unmelted hailstones still white on the planks of the bridge, at the thick layer of still-juicy, fleshy leaves heaped up around the stripped elm tree. Despite the gloom of nature around him, he felt unusually eager. The conversations he had been having with the peasants in the further village had shown that they were beginning to get used to their new arrangement. The old servant whose hut he had ducked into to dry off plainly approved of Levin's plan and had on his own initiative proposed joining the partnership by buying cattle.

"I only have to keep pushing stubbornly toward my aim, and I'll get there," Levin thought. "And it's something worth working for, worth taking trouble over. This isn't about me individually; the question of the public good comes into it. The whole system of farming — the chief factor in the condition of the people — has to be completely transformed. Instead of poverty, general prosperity and contentment; instead of hostility, harmony and shared interests. In short, a bloodless revolution — but a revolution of the greatest possible scale, starting in our little district, then the province, then Russia, then the whole world. Because a just idea can't help bearing fruit. Yes, this is an aim worth working for. And the fact that it's me — Kostya Levin, who went to a ball in a black tie and got turned down by the Shtcherbatskaya girl, and who, taken as a whole, is such a pitiful, worthless creature — that proves nothing. I'm sure Franklin felt just as worthless about himself, and he too had no faith in himself, taking himself as a whole. That means nothing. And he too probably had an Agafea Mihalovna to whom he confided his secrets."
Mulling over thoughts like these, Levin reached home in the dark.

The bailiff, back from the merchant, had brought part of the money for the wheat. An agreement had been settled with the old servant, and along the way the bailiff had learned that everywhere the corn was still standing in the fields, so that Levin's hundred and sixty shocks still uncarried were nothing compared to other people's losses.

After dinner Levin sat down in his armchair, as he usually did, with a book, and as he read he kept thinking about the journey ahead in connection with his book. Today the whole significance of the book stood out for him with unusual clarity, and whole sections lined themselves up in his mind as illustrations of his theories. "I must write that down," he thought. "That ought to form a brief introduction — which I'd thought unnecessary before." He got up to go to his writing-table, and Laska, lying at his feet, got up too, stretching and looking at him as if to ask which way they were going. But he had no time to write it down, because the head peasants had arrived, and Levin went out into the hall to see them.
After his levee — that is, after giving orders for the next day's work and dealing with all the peasants who had business with him — Levin went back to his study and sat down to work.
Laska lay under the table; Agafea Mihalovna settled into her usual spot with her knitting.
After he had been writing a little while, Levin suddenly thought, with unusual vividness, of Kitty — of her refusal, of their last meeting. He stood up and started pacing the room.
"What's the use of being gloomy?" said Agafea Mihalovna. "Come — why do you stay holed up at home? You ought to go to some warm springs, especially now you're all set for the trip."
"Well, I'm going the day after tomorrow, Agafea Mihalovna; I have to finish my work."

"There, there — your work, you say! As if you hadn't done enough for the peasants! Why, they're already saying, 'Your master is going to get some honor from the Tsar for it.' Funny thing, really — why need you worry yourself over the peasants?"
"I'm not worrying about them; I'm doing it for my own good."

Agafea Mihalovna knew every detail of Levin's plans for his land. Levin often laid out his views to her in their full complexity, and more than once he argued with her and did not agree with her comments. But this time she took what he had said entirely the wrong way.

"The salvation of one's soul is the one thing we all know we must think about before everything else," she said with a sigh. "Now, Parfen Denisitch — for all that he was no scholar — died the kind of death God grant any of us," she said, referring to a servant who had recently passed. "Took the sacrament and all."
"That's not what I mean," he said. "I mean I'm doing it for my own advantage. It's all the better for me if the peasants do their work better."
"Well, whatever you do, if a man's a lazy good-for-nothing, everything will be at sixes and sevens. If he has a conscience, he'll work; if not, there's no doing anything with him."
"Oh, come — you said yourself Ivan has started looking after the cattle better."
"All I say is," Agafea Mihalovna answered, plainly not speaking at random but in strict sequence, "that you ought to get married — that's what I say."

Agafea Mihalovna's pointing at the very subject he had just been thinking about hurt and stung him. Levin scowled, and without answering her sat back down to his work, repeating to himself everything he had been thinking about the real significance of that work. Only now and then he listened in the stillness to the click of Agafea Mihalovna's needles, and, remembering what he didn't want to remember, he frowned again.
At nine o'clock they heard the bell and the faint shake of a carriage coming over the mud.

"Well, here's visitors come to us — now you won't be dull," said Agafea Mihalovna, getting up and heading for the door. But Levin overtook her. His work wasn't going well now, and he was glad of a visitor, whoever it might be.

title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: Running halfway down the staircase, Levin caught a sound he knew — a familiar cough in the hall. But he heard it indistinctly through the sound of his own footsteps, and he hoped he was mistaken. Then he caught sight of a long, bony, familiar figure, and now it seemed there was no room for mistake; and yet he still kept hoping that this tall man pulling off his fur cloak and coughing was not his brother Nikolay.

Levin loved his brother, but being with him was always a strain. Just now, when Levin, under the influence of the thoughts that had come to him and Agafea Mihalovna's hint, was in a troubled and unsettled mood, the meeting with his brother that he had to face felt particularly hard. Instead of some lively, healthy outsider who would, he hoped, lift him out of his unsettled mood, he had to see the brother who knew him through and through, who would draw out all the thoughts closest to his heart and force him to show himself completely. And that he wasn't ready to do.

Angry with himself for so low a feeling, Levin ran into the hall; the moment he had seen his brother up close, the feeling of selfish disappointment vanished and was replaced by pity. As terrible as Nikolay had looked before in his emaciation and sickness, he looked still more emaciated now, still more wasted. He was a skeleton covered in skin.

He stood in the hall, jerking his long thin neck and pulling the scarf off it, and gave a strange, pitiful smile. When Levin saw that smile — submissive and humble — he felt something clutch at his throat.

"You see, I've come to you," Nikolay said in a thick voice, never for a second taking his eyes off his brother's face. "I've been meaning to a long while, but I've been unwell the whole time. Now I'm much better," he said, rubbing his beard with his big, thin hands.
"Yes, yes!" Levin answered. And he felt even more frightened when, kissing him, he felt the dryness of his brother's skin on his lips and saw, up close, his big eyes lit with a strange light.

A few weeks earlier, Konstantin Levin had written to his brother that with the sale of the small piece of property that had stayed undivided, there were about two thousand roubles coming to him as his share.

Nikolay said he had come now to collect this money and, more importantly, to spend some time in the old nest, to get back in touch with the earth and renew his strength like the heroes of old for the work that lay ahead. In spite of his exaggerated stoop and the emaciation that was so striking on a frame of his height, his movements were as quick and abrupt as ever. Levin led him into his study.
His brother dressed with particular care — something he had never used to do — combed his thin, lank hair, and, smiling, went upstairs.

He was in the most affectionate and good-humored mood, just as Levin often remembered him from childhood. He even mentioned Sergey Ivanovitch without bitterness. When he saw Agafea Mihalovna he joked with her and asked after the old servants. The news of Parfen Denisitch's death made a painful impression on him. A look of fear crossed his face, but he was himself again at once.

"Of course he was quite old," he said, and changed the subject. "Well, I'll spend a month or two with you and then I'm off to Moscow. Do you know, Myakov has promised me a place there, and I'm going into the service. I'm going to arrange my life completely differently now," he went on. "You know, I got rid of that woman."
"Marya Nikolaevna? Why, what for?"

"Oh, she was a horrid woman! She caused me all sorts of trouble." But he didn't say what the trouble was. He couldn't say he had thrown Marya Nikolaevna out because the tea was weak, and, above all, because she would fuss over him as if he were an invalid.

"Besides, I want to turn over a new leaf completely now. I've done foolish things, of course, like everyone else, but money's the last consideration; I don't regret that. So long as there's health — and my health, thank God, is fully restored."

Levin listened and racked his brains, but couldn't think of anything to say. Nikolay probably felt the same; he began questioning his brother about his affairs, and Levin was glad to talk about himself, because at least there he could speak without hypocrisy. He told his brother about his plans and what he was doing.
His brother listened, but plainly wasn't interested.
These two men were so close, so akin to each other, that the slightest gesture or tone of voice told both of them more than any words could.

Both of them now had only one thought — Nikolay's illness and the nearness of his death — and it smothered everything else. But neither of them dared mention it, and so whatever they did say — not voicing the one thought filling their minds — was all a lie. Levin had never been so glad when the evening ended and it was time for bed. Never with any outsider, never on any formal visit had he been so unnatural and false as he was that evening. And the awareness of this unnaturalness, and the remorse he felt at it, only made him more unnatural. He wanted to weep over his dying, dearly loved brother, and he had to sit and listen and keep talking about how he meant to live.
The house was damp, and only the one bedroom had been kept heated; Levin made up a bed for his brother behind a screen in his own room.

His brother got into bed, and whether he slept or didn't sleep, he tossed about like a sick man, coughed, and when he couldn't get his throat clear mumbled something. Sometimes when his breathing was painful he said, "Oh, my God!" Sometimes when he was choking he muttered angrily, "Ah, the devil!" Levin couldn't sleep for a long while, listening to him. His thoughts went in every direction, but the end of every thought was the same — death. Death, the inevitable end of everything, for the first time presented itself to him with overwhelming force. And death, which was here in this beloved brother, half-asleep and groaning and habitually calling on God and the devil without distinction, no longer seemed so remote as it had until now. It was in him too — he felt that. If not today, then tomorrow; if not tomorrow, then in thirty years — wasn't it all the same? And what this inevitable death actually was — he didn't know, had never thought about it, and what was worse, hadn't the strength, hadn't the courage to think about it.
"I work, I want to do something, but I had forgotten that it all has to end; I had forgotten — death."

He sat on his bed in the dark, hunched up, hugging his knees, and, holding his breath from the strain of thinking, he turned it over. But the harder he thought, the clearer it became to him that, undeniably, in actual fact, in looking at life he had forgotten one small fact — that death will come, and all of it ends; that nothing was even worth beginning, and there was no helping it anyway. Yes, it was awful, but there it was.

"But I'm still alive. Now what's to be done? What's to be done?" he said in despair. He lit a candle, got up cautiously, and went to the looking-glass, and started studying his face and hair. Yes, there were gray hairs at his temples. He opened his mouth. His back teeth were beginning to rot. He bared his muscular arms. Yes, there was strength in them. But Nikolay, lying there breathing with what was left of his lungs, had had a strong, healthy body too. And suddenly he remembered how as children they used to go to bed together, and how they only waited for Fyodor Bogdanitch to be out of the room before flinging pillows at each other and laughing — laughing so helplessly that even their awe of Fyodor Bogdanitch couldn't check the rising, overflowing sense of life and happiness. "And now that bent, hollow chest... and I, not knowing what will become of me, or what for..."
"K... ha! K... ha! Damnation! Why do you keep fidgeting? Why don't you go to sleep?" his brother's voice called over to him.
"Oh, I don't know — I'm not sleepy."
"I've had a good sleep — I'm not in a sweat now. Here, feel my shirt; it's not wet, is it?"

Levin felt it, then slipped back behind the screen and blew out the candle, but for a long while he couldn't sleep. The question of how to live had only just begun to clear up for him a little when a new, unanswerable question presented itself — death.
"Why — he's dying — yes, he'll be dead by spring, and how can I help him? What can I say to him? What do I know about it? I'd even forgotten there was such a thing."

title: Chapter 32
paragraphs: Levin had noticed long ago that when people make you uncomfortable by being excessively pliant and meek, you very soon find them unbearable for being touchy and irritable. He felt this was how things would go with his brother. And in fact Nikolay's gentleness did not hold up long. The very next morning he turned irritable and seemed bent on picking fights with his brother, going after him on his tenderest points.

Levin felt to blame and couldn't put things right. He felt that if they had both dropped the pretense and spoken — as the saying goes — from the heart, meaning if they had said only what they were actually thinking and feeling, they would simply have looked into each other's faces, and Konstantin could only have said, "You're dying, you're dying!" and Nikolay could only have answered, "I know I'm dying, but I'm afraid, I'm afraid, I'm afraid!" And nothing more could have been said, if they were saying only what was in their hearts. But life like that was impossible, and so Konstantin tried to do what he had been trying to do all his life and never could learn — what so many people, as far as he could see, knew how to do so well, and without which there was no living at all. He tried to say what he wasn't thinking, and felt all the while that it rang false, that his brother caught him at it and was exasperated.
On the third day Nikolay drew his brother into explaining his scheme again, and began not just attacking it but deliberately confounding it with communism.
"You've simply borrowed an idea that isn't yours, and you've distorted it, and you're trying to apply it where it doesn't apply."

"But I'm telling you, it has nothing to do with it. They deny the justice of property, of capital, of inheritance, while I don't deny this chief stimulus." (Levin felt disgusted with himself for using such expressions, but ever since he had been absorbed in his work, he had unconsciously been reaching more and more often for foreign, un-Russian words.) "All I want is to regulate labor."
"Which means you've borrowed an idea, stripped it of everything that gave it any force, and want to pass it off as something new," Nikolay said, tugging angrily at his necktie.
"But my idea has nothing in common...."

"At least that idea," said Nikolay Levin, with an ironical smile, his eyes flashing maliciously, "has the charm of — what shall I call it? — geometrical symmetry, of clearness, of definiteness. It may be a Utopia. But once you grant the possibility of making a _tabula rasa_ of the entire past — no property, no family — then labor would organize itself. But you gain nothing...."
"Why do you mix things up? I've never been a communist."
"But I have been, and I think it's premature but rational, and that it has a future, just like Christianity in its first centuries."
"All I'm maintaining is that the labor force ought to be investigated from the point of view of natural science — that is, studied, its qualities ascertained...."

"But that's a complete waste of time. That force finds its own form of activity according to the stage of its development. There were slaves first, everywhere; then sharecroppers; and now we have the half-crop system, rent, and day laborers. What are you trying to find?"

Levin suddenly lost his temper at this, because at the bottom of his heart he was afraid it was true — true that he was trying to hold the balance between communism and the familiar forms, and that this was barely possible.
"I'm trying to find a way of working productively, for myself and for the laborers. I want to organize...." he answered heatedly.
"You don't want to organize anything; you just want, the way you've always wanted, to be original — to pose as someone who doesn't simply exploit the peasants but has an idea behind it."
"All right, that's what you think — now leave me alone!" Levin answered, feeling the muscles of his left cheek twitch uncontrollably.
"You've never had convictions, and you don't have any now; you only want to flatter your vanity."
"Fine, then; leave me alone!"
"And I will leave you alone! and it's high time I did, and to the devil with you, and I'm sorry I ever came!"
Despite all Levin's efforts to calm his brother afterward, Nikolay would hear none of it, insisting it was better to part — and Konstantin saw it was simply that life had become unbearable to him.
Nikolay was just getting ready to go when Konstantin went in to him again and asked him, rather unnaturally, to forgive him if he had hurt his feelings in any way.
"Ah, magnanimity!" said Nikolay, and he smiled. "If you want to be right, I can give you that satisfaction. You're right; but I'm going all the same."
Only at the very moment of parting did Nikolay kiss him, and looking suddenly, strangely, and seriously at his brother, he said:

"Anyway, don't think badly of me, Kostya!" — and his voice quivered. Those were the only words spoken sincerely between them. Levin knew they meant, "You see, you know, that I'm in a bad way, and perhaps we shall not see each other again." Levin knew it, and the tears poured from his eyes. He kissed his brother once more, but he couldn't speak, and didn't know what to say.
Three days after his brother's departure, Levin too set off on his foreign tour. Running into Shtcherbatsky, Kitty's cousin, on the train, Levin astonished him by his depression.
"What's the matter with you?" Shtcherbatsky asked him.
"Oh, nothing; there isn't much happiness in life."
"Not much? Come with me to Paris instead of Mulhausen. I'll show you how to be happy."
"No, I'm done with all that. It's time I was dead."
"Now there's a good one!" Shtcherbatsky said, laughing. "Why, I'm only just getting ready to begin."
"Yes, I thought the same not long ago — but now I know I'll soon be dead."
