Levin was saying what he had honestly been thinking lately. He saw nothing but death, or the approach toward death, in everything. But his cherished scheme only absorbed him the more. Life had to be got through somehow until death came. Darkness had fallen over everything for him; but precisely because of this darkness he felt that the one guiding thread in it was his work, and he gripped it and clung to it with all his strength.
PART FOUR

title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Karenins, husband and wife, went on living in the same house, met every day, and remained complete strangers to each other. Alexey Alexandrovitch made a rule of seeing his wife each day so that the servants would have no grounds for suspicion, but he avoided dining at home. Vronsky never came to Alexey Alexandrovitch's house, but Anna saw him elsewhere, and her husband knew it.

The position was wretched for all three of them, and not one of them could have endured it for a single day if they hadn't expected it to change — if they hadn't believed it was only a temporary, painful ordeal that would pass. Alexey Alexandrovitch hoped that this passion would pass, the way everything passes, that everyone would forget about it, and that his name would remain unblemished. Anna, on whom the situation depended and for whom it was more miserable than for anyone, endured it because she not only hoped but firmly believed that it would all very soon be settled and come out right. She had no idea what would resolve it, but she was sure something would turn up before long. Vronsky, against his own will or wishes, followed her lead, and hoped too that something — apart from anything he himself did — would surely sort it all out.

In the middle of winter Vronsky spent a tedious week. A foreign prince had come to Petersburg on a visit and had been placed in his charge, with Vronsky responsible for showing him the sights. Vronsky cut a distinguished figure; he had the knack of behaving with respectful dignity and was used to dealing with such grand personages — which is why he had been given the prince. But he found the duty very tiresome. The prince was anxious not to miss anything that he might be asked about back home — had he seen this in Russia? — and on his own account he was determined to enjoy every Russian amusement to the full. Vronsky had to be his guide in satisfying both impulses. Mornings they spent driving out to see the sights; evenings they spent enjoying the national entertainments. The prince enjoyed health exceptional even by royal standards. Through gymnastics and careful attention to his condition he had brought himself to the point where, in spite of his excesses in pleasure, he looked as fresh as a big, glossy green Dutch cucumber. The prince had traveled a great deal, and counted as one of the chief advantages of modern transport the accessibility of the pleasures of every nation.

He had been in Spain, where he had indulged in serenades and made friends with a Spanish girl who played the mandolin. In Switzerland he had killed chamois. In England he had ridden in a red coat over hedges and shot two hundred pheasants for a bet. In Turkey he had got into a harem; in India he had hunted on the back of an elephant; and now in Russia he wished to taste all the specifically Russian forms of pleasure.

Vronsky, who was effectively his master of ceremonies, took great pains to arrange all the Russian entertainments suggested for the prince by various people. They had race horses and Russian pancakes and bear hunts and three-horse sledges and gypsies and drinking parties with the Russian accompaniment of broken crockery. And the prince fell in with the Russian spirit with astonishing ease, smashed trays of crockery, sat with a gypsy girl on his knee, and seemed to be asking — what more, and does the whole Russian spirit really come down to just this?

In reality, of all the Russian entertainments the prince liked best French actresses, ballet dancers, and white-seal champagne. Vronsky was used to princes, but either because he himself had changed lately, or because he was in too close proximity to this prince, the week felt dreadfully tiresome. The whole week he felt the way a man might feel set to look after a dangerous madman — afraid of the madman, and at the same time, from being constantly with him, afraid for his own sanity. Vronsky was continually aware that he couldn't relax for a second from the tone of stern, official respect, or he himself might be the one insulted. The prince's manner toward the very people who, to Vronsky's surprise, were ready to stoop to any depth to provide him with Russian amusements was contemptuous. His comments on the Russian women he was supposedly there to study made Vronsky flush with indignation more than once. The chief reason the prince was so particularly disagreeable to Vronsky was that he couldn't help seeing himself in him. And what he saw in this mirror did not flatter his self-esteem. Here was a very stupid, very self-satisfied, very healthy, very well-washed man, and nothing more. He was a gentleman — true, and Vronsky couldn't deny it. He was even-tempered and not obsequious with his superiors, free and engaging with his equals, and contemptuously indulgent with his inferiors. Vronsky was the same, and considered it a great merit. But to this prince he was an inferior, and the prince's contemptuously indulgent manner toward him revolted him.
"Brainless beef! Can I really be like that?" he thought.

Be that as it might, when on the seventh day he parted from the prince, who was setting off for Moscow, and received his thanks, he was happy to be rid of his uncomfortable position and the unpleasant reflection of himself. He said goodbye at the station on their return from a bear hunt where they had been treated to a display of Russian prowess that had gone on all night.

title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: When he got home, Vronsky found a note from Anna waiting. She wrote: "I am ill and unhappy. I can't come out, but I can't go any longer without seeing you. Come this evening. Alexey Alexandrovitch goes to the council at seven and will be there till ten." He paused for a moment over the strangeness of her telling him to come straight to her, in spite of her husband's insistence that she not receive him, then decided to go.

Vronsky had gotten his promotion that winter; he was now a colonel, had left the regimental quarters, and was living on his own. After a quick lunch he lay down on the sofa, and within five minutes memories of the hideous scenes he had witnessed over the past few days blurred together with a mental image of Anna and of the peasant who had played such a part in the bear hunt, and Vronsky fell asleep. He woke in the dark, trembling with horror, and hurriedly lit a candle. "What was that? What? What was the terrible thing I dreamed? Yes, yes — I think a little dirty man with a disheveled beard was stooping over, doing something, and all at once he began saying some strange words in French. Yes — there was nothing else in the dream," he said to himself. "But why was it so awful?" He saw the peasant again, vividly, and the incomprehensible French words the peasant had spoken, and a chill of horror ran down his back.
"What nonsense!" Vronsky thought, and looked at his watch.

It was already half past eight. He rang for his servant, dressed in a hurry, and went out onto the steps, forgetting the dream entirely and worried only about being late. As he drove up to the Karenins' entrance he looked at his watch and saw it was ten minutes to nine. A high, narrow carriage with a pair of grays stood at the door. He recognized Anna's carriage. "She's coming to me," Vronsky thought, "and better that she should. I don't like going into that house. But no matter; I can't hide." And with that manner he had had since boyhood, of a man who has nothing to be ashamed of, Vronsky stepped out of his sledge and went to the door. The door opened, and the hall-porter with a rug on his arm called the carriage forward. Vronsky, though he didn't usually notice small things, noticed at that moment the amazed look the porter shot at him. In the doorway itself Vronsky nearly collided with Alexey Alexandrovitch. The gas jet threw its full light on the bloodless, sunken face under the black hat and on the white cravat shining against the beaver of the coat. Karenin's fixed, dull eyes were fastened on Vronsky's face. Vronsky bowed, and Alexey Alexandrovitch, chewing his lips, lifted his hand to his hat and walked on. Vronsky watched, without turning his head, as he got into the carriage, picked up the rug and the opera-glass from the window, and disappeared. Vronsky went into the hall. His brows were knotted, and his eyes glittered with a proud, angry light.

"What a position!" he thought. "If he would fight, if he would stand up for his honor, I could act, I could express what I feel; but this weakness or baseness.... He puts me in the position of playing false, which I never meant and never mean to do."

Vronsky's thinking had changed since the day of his conversation with Anna in the Vrede garden. Unconsciously yielding to Anna's weakness — she had surrendered herself completely to him and simply looked to him to decide her fate, ready to submit to anything — he had long since stopped thinking their tie might end as he had thought back then. His ambitious plans had retreated into the background again, and feeling that he had stepped outside the circle of activity in which everything was definite, he had given himself entirely to his passion, and that passion was binding him more and more closely to her.
He was still in the hall when he caught the sound of her retreating footsteps. He knew she had been waiting for him, listening for him, and was now going back to the drawing-room.
"No," she cried when she saw him, and at the first sound of her voice the tears came into her eyes. "No; if it's going to go on like this, the end will come much, much too soon."
"What is it, dearest?"

"What? I've been waiting in agony for an hour, two hours.... No, I won't.... I can't quarrel with you. Of course you couldn't come. No, I won't." She laid her two hands on his shoulders and looked at him for a long time with a deep, passionate, searching look. She was studying his face to make up for the time she had not seen him. Every time she saw him, she was bringing the picture of him she carried in her imagination (incomparably better, impossible in reality) into line with him as he really was.

title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: "You met him?" she asked when they had sat down at the table in the lamplight. "You see — that's your punishment for being late."
"Yes; but how was it? Wasn't he supposed to be at the council?"
"He had been and come back, and was going out somewhere again. But that doesn't matter. Don't talk about it. Where were you? With the prince, still?"

She knew every detail of his life. He was about to say that he had been up all night and had fallen asleep, but looking at her excited, rapturous face, he was ashamed. So he said he had had to go and report on the prince's departure.
"But it's over now? He's gone?"
"Thank God it's over! You wouldn't believe how unbearable it's been for me."

"Why? Isn't it the life all of you, all young men, always lead?" she said, drawing her brows together, and taking up the crochet work that lay on the table she began drawing the hook out of it without looking at Vronsky.

"I gave that life up long ago," he said, surprised at the change in her face and trying to make out what it meant. "And I'll admit," he added, with a smile that showed his thick, white teeth, "this week I've been looking at myself, as it were, in a mirror, seeing that life — and I didn't like it."
She held the work in her hands but did not crochet, and looked at him with strange, shining, hostile eyes.
"Liza came to see me this morning — they're not afraid to call on me, in spite of Countess Lidia Ivanovna," she put in — "and she told me about your Athenian evening. How disgusting!"
"I was just about to say...."
She cut him off. "It was that Thérèse you used to know?"
"I was just saying...."

"How disgusting you men are! How can you not understand that a woman never forgets that," she said, getting angrier and more obvious about the cause of her irritation, "especially a woman who can't know your life? What do I know? What have I ever known?" she went on, "only what you tell me. And how do I know if you tell me the truth?..."
"Anna, you hurt me. Don't you trust me? Haven't I told you that I haven't a thought I wouldn't lay bare to you?"
"Yes, yes," she said, plainly trying to suppress her jealous thoughts. "But if you only knew how miserable I am! I believe you, I believe you.... What were you saying?"

But he couldn't immediately recall what he had been going to say. These fits of jealousy, which had been growing more and more frequent in her lately, horrified him, and however much he tried to hide it, they made him feel cold toward her — even though he knew the cause of her jealousy was her love for him. How many times had he told himself that her love was happiness; and now she loved him as a woman can love when love has outweighed all the good things of life — and he was far further from happiness than when he had followed her from Moscow. Back then he had thought himself unhappy, but happiness lay ahead of him; now he felt that the best happiness was already behind him. She was completely unlike what she had been when he first saw her. Both morally and physically she had changed for the worse. She had broadened out all over, and at the moment when she was talking about the actress her face wore an evil look of hatred that disfigured it. He looked at her the way a man looks at a faded flower he has picked, barely recognizing in it the beauty for which he had picked it and ruined it. And in spite of this he felt that back then, when his love was stronger, he could, if he had really wanted to, have torn that love out of his heart; but now, when at this very moment it seemed to him he felt no love for her, he knew that what bound him to her could not be broken.

"Well, then, what was it you were going to say about the prince? I've driven away the fiend," she added. The fiend was their name for her jealousy. "What did you start telling me about the prince? Why did you find it so tedious?"

"Oh, it was unbearable!" he said, trying to pick up the thread of his interrupted thought. "He doesn't improve on closer acquaintance. If you want a definition, here it is: a prime, well-fed beast of the sort that takes medals at cattle shows, and nothing more," he said, in a tone of vexation that caught her interest.
"No; how so?" she replied. "He's seen a great deal, anyway — he's cultured?"
"It's a completely different culture — their culture. He's been cultivated, you can see, simply so as to be able to despise culture, the way they despise everything but animal pleasures."
"But don't all of you care for these animal pleasures?" she said, and again he noticed a dark look in her eyes avoiding his.
"Why are you defending him?" he said, smiling.

"I'm not defending him, it's nothing to me; but I imagine that if you hadn't cared for those pleasures yourself, you could have gotten out of them. But if it gives you pleasure to gaze at Thérèse in the costume of Eve...."
"The devil — again," Vronsky said, taking the hand she had laid on the table and kissing it.

"Yes, but I can't help it. You don't know what I went through waiting for you. I don't think I'm jealous. I'm not jealous: I believe you when you're here; but when you're away somewhere, leading your life, which is so incomprehensible to me...."

She turned away from him, finally pulled the hook out of the crochet work, and rapidly, helped by her forefinger, began working loop after loop of wool that gleamed dazzlingly white in the lamplight, her slender wrist moving quickly, nervously, in the embroidered cuff.
"How did it happen, then? Where did you run into Alexey Alexandrovitch?" Her voice rang in an unnatural, jarring tone.
"We bumped into each other in the doorway."
"And he bowed to you like this?"

She lengthened her face, half-closed her eyes, transformed her expression in an instant, folded her hands, and Vronsky suddenly saw in her beautiful face the very expression with which Alexey Alexandrovitch had bowed to him. He smiled, while she laughed gaily, with that sweet, deep laugh that was one of her greatest charms.

"I don't understand him at all," Vronsky said. "If after your confession at your country house he had broken with you, if he had called me out — but this I can't understand. How can he tolerate such a position? He feels it, that's obvious."
"Him?" she said with a sneer. "He's perfectly content."
"What are we all miserable about, when everything could be so happy?"

"Not him. Don't I know him, and the falsity he's utterly soaked in?... Could anyone with feeling live the way he lives with me? He understands nothing, feels nothing. Could a man with any feeling live in the same house with his unfaithful wife? Could he talk to her, call her 'my dear'?"
And again she couldn't help mimicking him: "'Anna, _ma chère_; Anna, dear!'"

"He's not a man, not a human being — he's a doll! No one knows him, but I know him. Oh, if I had been in his place, I would have killed long ago, would have torn to pieces a wife like me. I wouldn't have said, 'Anna, _ma chère_'! He's not a man, he's an official machine. He doesn't understand that I'm your wife, that he's outside of it, that he's superfluous.... Let's not talk about him!..."

"You're unfair, very unfair, dearest," Vronsky said, trying to calm her. "But never mind, let's not talk about him. Tell me what you've been doing? What's the matter? What has been wrong with you, and what did the doctor say?"
She looked at him with mocking amusement. Clearly she had hit on other absurd and grotesque sides of her husband and was waiting for a moment to come out with them.
But he went on:
"I think it isn't illness — it's your condition. When will it be?"
The ironical light faded from her eyes, but a different smile, the consciousness of something he didn't know what, and of quiet sadness, came over her face.

"Soon, soon. You say our position is miserable, that we have to put an end to it. If you only knew how terrible it is to me, what I would give to be able to love you freely and openly! I wouldn't torture myself, or torture you with my jealousy.... And it will come soon, but not the way we expect."

And at the thought of how it would come, she felt so pitiable to herself that tears came into her eyes, and she couldn't go on. She laid her hand on his sleeve, dazzling and white in the lamplight, with its rings.
"It won't come the way we suppose. I didn't mean to say this to you, but you've made me. Soon, soon, it will all be over, and we will all, all be at peace, and suffer no more."
"I don't understand," he said, understanding her perfectly.

"You asked when. Soon. And I won't live through it. Don't interrupt me!" — and she hurried to speak. "I know it; I know it for certain. I will die; and I'm very glad I'll die, and release myself and you."
Tears dropped from her eyes; he bent over her hand and began kissing it, trying to hide the emotion he felt — which, he knew, had no grounds at all, though he couldn't control it.
"Yes, it's better that way," she said, gripping his hand tightly. "That's the only way, the only way left to us."
He had recovered himself and lifted his head.
"How absurd! What absurd nonsense you're talking!"
"No, it's the truth."
"What, what's the truth?"
"That I'm going to die. I had a dream."
"A dream?" Vronsky repeated, and instantly recalled the peasant in his own dream.

"Yes, a dream," she said. "It's a long time since I dreamed it. I dreamed I ran into my bedroom, that I had to get something there, find out something; you know how it is in dreams," she said, her eyes wide with horror; "and in the bedroom, in the corner, something was standing."
"Oh, what nonsense! How can you believe...."
But she would not let him interrupt her. What she was saying mattered too much to her.

"And the something turned around, and I saw it was a peasant with a disheveled beard, little, and dreadful looking. I wanted to run away, but he bent down over a sack and was fumbling there with his hands...."
She showed how he had moved his hands. Terror was in her face. And Vronsky, remembering his own dream, felt the same terror filling his soul.

"He was fumbling and kept talking quickly, quickly in French, you know: _Il faut le battre, le fer, le broyer, le pétrir_.... And in my horror I tried to wake up, and I woke up — but woke up inside the dream. And I began asking myself what it meant. And Korney said to me: 'In childbirth you'll die, ma'am, you'll die....' And then I woke up."
"What nonsense, what nonsense!" Vronsky said; but he felt himself that there was no conviction in his voice.
"But let's not talk about it. Ring the bell, I'll have tea. And stay a little longer now; it won't be long that I shall...."

But all at once she stopped. The expression on her face changed in an instant. Horror and excitement were suddenly replaced by a look of soft, solemn, blissful attention. He couldn't grasp the meaning of the change. She was listening to the stirring of the new life within her.

title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: Alexey Alexandrovitch, after running into Vronsky on his own steps, drove on, as he had intended, to the Italian opera. He sat through two acts and saw everyone he had wanted to see. On returning home, he carefully looked over the hat stand, and noticing that no military overcoat was there, he went, as usual, to his room. But, contrary to his habit, he did not go to bed; he paced his study until three in the morning. The feeling of furious anger with his wife — who would not observe the proprieties and keep the one condition he had set on her, not to receive her lover in her own home — gave him no peace. She had not complied with his demand, and he was bound to punish her and carry out his threat — obtain a divorce and take away his son. He knew all the difficulties tied to this course, but he had said he would do it, and now he had to follow through. Countess Lidia Ivanovna had hinted that this was the best way out of his position, and lately the obtaining of divorces had been brought to such perfection that Alexey Alexandrovitch saw a way of overcoming the procedural obstacles. Misfortunes never come singly, and the affairs of the reorganization of the native tribes, and the irrigation of the lands of Zaraisky province, had brought such official troubles down on Alexey Alexandrovitch that he had been in a state of continual extreme irritation for some time.

He didn't sleep at all that night, and his fury, growing in a sort of vast arithmetical progression, reached its peak by morning. He dressed in a hurry, and as if carrying a cup full of wrath, afraid of spilling any, afraid of losing along with his wrath the energy he needed for the interview with his wife, he went into her room the moment he heard she was up.

Anna, who thought she knew her husband so well, was amazed at his appearance when he came in. His brow was lowering, and his eyes stared darkly past her, avoiding her gaze; his mouth was tightly and contemptuously shut. In his walk, in his gestures, in the sound of his voice there was a determination and firmness his wife had never seen in him. He went into her room and, without greeting her, walked straight to her writing-table, took her keys, and opened a drawer.
"What do you want?" she cried.
"Your lover's letters," he said.

"They're not here," she said, shutting the drawer; but from the action he saw he had guessed right, and roughly shoving her hand away, he quickly snatched up a portfolio in which he knew she kept her most important papers. She tried to pull the portfolio away, but he pushed her back.

"Sit down! I have to speak to you," he said, putting the portfolio under his arm and squeezing it so tightly with his elbow that his shoulder lifted. Amazed and intimidated, she stared at him in silence.
"I told you I would not allow you to receive your lover in this house."
"I had to see him to...."
She broke off, unable to find a reason.
"I do not go into the details of why a woman wants to see her lover."
"I meant, I only...." she said, flushing hotly. His coarseness angered her and gave her courage. "Surely you must feel how easy it is for you to insult me?" she said.
"An honest man and an honest woman can be insulted, but to call a thief a thief is simply _la constatation d'un fait_."
"This cruelty is something new — I didn't know it in you."
"You call it cruelty for a husband to give his wife liberty, granting her the honorable protection of his name, simply on the condition of observing the proprieties: is that cruelty?"
"It's worse than cruel — it's base, if you want to know!" Anna cried, in a rush of hatred, and getting up, she started to walk away.

"No!" he shrieked, in his shrill voice, which pitched a note higher than usual, and his big hands clutched her arm so violently that red marks were left from the bracelet he was squeezing, and he forced her back into her seat.
"Base! If you want to use that word, what is base is to abandon husband and child for a lover while you eat your husband's bread!"

She bowed her head. She did not say what she had said to her lover the evening before — that _he_ was her husband, and her husband was superfluous; she didn't even think it. She felt the full justice of his words, and only said softly:
"You cannot describe my position as worse than I feel it to be myself; but what are you saying all this for?"

"What am I saying it for? what for?" he went on, just as angrily. "So that you may know that since you haven't carried out my wishes about observing outward decorum, I will take measures to put an end to this state of affairs."
"Soon, very soon, it will end on its own," she said; and again, at the thought of death near at hand and now desired, tears came into her eyes.
"It will end sooner than you and your lover have planned! If you must have the satisfaction of animal passion...."
"Alexey Alexandrovitch! I won't say it's not generous, but it isn't like a gentleman to strike someone who's down."
"Yes, you only think of yourself! But the sufferings of the man who was your husband don't interest you. You don't care that his whole life is ruined, that he is thuff... thuff...."

Alexey Alexandrovitch was speaking so quickly that he stammered, and was utterly unable to get out the word "suffering." In the end he pronounced it "thuffering." She wanted to laugh, and was immediately ashamed that anything could amuse her at such a moment. And for the first time, for an instant, she felt for him, put herself in his place, and was sorry for him. But what could she say or do? Her head sank and she sat in silence. He too was silent for a while, then began to speak in a frigid, less shrill voice, stressing random words that carried no special meaning.
"I came to tell you...." he said.

She glanced up at him. "No, it was my imagination," she thought, remembering the expression on his face when he stumbled over the word "suffering." "No; can a man with those dull eyes, with that self-satisfied complacency, feel anything?"
"I cannot change anything," she whispered.

"I have come to tell you that I am going tomorrow to Moscow, and will not return to this house again, and you will receive notice of what I decide through the lawyer into whose hands I am putting the business of getting a divorce. My son is going to my sister's," said Alexey Alexandrovitch, recalling with an effort what he had meant to say about his son.
"You're taking Seryozha to hurt me," she said, looking at him from under her brows. "You don't love him.... Leave Seryozha with me!"
"Yes, I have lost even my affection for my son, because he is connected with the revulsion I feel for you. Still, I'll take him. Good-bye!"
And he was leaving, but now she held him back.
"Alexey Alexandrovitch, leave Seryozha with me!" she whispered once more. "I have nothing else to say. Leave Seryozha until my... I shall soon be confined; leave him with me!"
Alexey Alexandrovitch flew into a rage, snatched his hand away from her, and left the room without a word.

title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: The waiting room of the celebrated Petersburg lawyer was full when Alexey Alexandrovitch walked in. Three women — an elderly lady, a young one, and a merchant's wife — and three men — a German banker with a ring on his finger, a bearded merchant, and a furious-looking government clerk in official uniform with a cross at his neck — had clearly been waiting a long while already. Two clerks sat at tables scratching away with their pens. The fittings on the writing tables, of which Alexey Alexandrovitch himself was very particular, were unusually fine. He noticed it in spite of himself. One of the clerks, without standing up, turned on him with a half-closed glare. "What is it you want?"
He answered that he had come to see the lawyer on a matter of business.
"He's busy," the clerk said curtly, and pointed his pen at the people waiting before going back to his writing.
"Could he not spare me a moment?" Alexey Alexandrovitch asked.
"He has no free time — he is always busy. Kindly take your turn."
"Then I must trouble you to take in my card," Alexey Alexandrovitch said with dignity, realizing there was no way to remain anonymous.
The clerk took the card and, plainly not pleased by what he read, went off to the inner door.

Alexey Alexandrovitch was in principle a supporter of open legal proceedings, though for certain higher official reasons he disliked the way the principle was applied in Russia and disapproved of it — as far as one could disapprove of anything established by authority of the Emperor. His entire career had been spent in administration, and so, whenever he found fault with something, his disapproval was always softened by the awareness that mistakes were inevitable and that reform was possible in every department. In the new public courts he disliked the restrictions placed on the lawyers conducting cases. But until now he had had no personal contact with the courts, and his disapproval of their openness had been purely theoretical; now it was reinforced by the disagreeable impression made on him by the lawyer's waiting room.
"He'll be with you in a moment," the clerk said; and two minutes later the bulky figure of an old solicitor who had been consulting with the lawyer did indeed appear in the doorway.

The lawyer was a short, squat, bald man with a dark reddish beard, long pale eyebrows, and a heavy overhanging brow. He was dressed as though for a wedding — from his cravat down to his double watch chain and his polished boots. His face was shrewd and manly, but his clothes were dandyish and in poor taste.
"Please come in," the lawyer said, addressing Alexey Alexandrovitch, and ushered him gloomily ahead before closing the door.

"Won't you sit down?" He gestured to an armchair beside a writing table piled with papers. He sat down himself and, rubbing his small short-fingered hands — the backs of them covered with white hairs — tilted his head to one side. He had barely settled into that posture when a moth flew across the table. With a quickness no one would have guessed at, the lawyer flung out his hands, caught the moth, and resumed his position.

"Before I go into my business," Alexey Alexandrovitch said, watching the lawyer's movements with astonished eyes, "I should mention that the matter I have to speak about must be kept strictly private."
The lawyer's heavy reddish mustache parted in a barely perceptible smile.
"I should not be a lawyer if I couldn't keep the secrets entrusted to me. But if you would like assurance...."
Alexey Alexandrovitch glanced at his face and saw that the shrewd gray eyes were laughing — and looked as though they already knew the whole story.
"You know my name?" Alexey Alexandrovitch went on.
"I know you and the fine" — he caught another moth — "work you do, like every Russian," said the lawyer, bowing.
Alexey Alexandrovitch drew a breath and steadied himself. But once he had decided, he went on in his shrill voice, without timidity or hesitation, putting weight on a word here and there.

"I have had the misfortune," Alexey Alexandrovitch began, "to be deceived in my marriage, and I wish to end all ties with my wife by legal means — that is, by divorce — but in such a way that my son will not remain with his mother."

The lawyer's gray eyes did their best not to laugh, but they were dancing with irrepressible glee, and Alexey Alexandrovitch saw it was not simply the satisfaction of a man who had landed a profitable case: there was triumph and elation in them, a gleam like the malicious glint he had seen in his wife's eyes.
"You wish my help in obtaining a divorce?"

"Yes, precisely; but I must warn you that I may be wasting your time and attention. I have come only to consult you as a first step. I want a divorce, but the form in which it can be obtained is of great importance to me. It's quite possible that if that form does not suit my requirements, I will give up the idea of a legal divorce."
"Oh, that's always how it is," the lawyer said, "and that is always for you to decide."

He let his eyes drop to Alexey Alexandrovitch's feet, feeling he might give offense if his client caught sight of the amusement he could not suppress. A moth fluttered past his nose; he twitched his hands but held back from catching it out of respect for Alexey Alexandrovitch's situation.

"Although the general outlines of our laws on this subject are known to me," Alexey Alexandrovitch went on, "I should be glad to have some sense of the forms in which such things are handled in practice."

"You would be glad," the lawyer answered, eyes still down, taking up his client's manner of speech with a certain satisfaction, "for me to set out for you all the means by which you could achieve what you want?"
And on receiving a confirming nod from Alexey Alexandrovitch, he went on, stealing a glance now and then at the face opposite him, which was turning red in patches.

"Under our laws," he said, with a faint hint of disapproval of those laws, "divorce is possible, as you know, in the following cases.... One moment!" he called to a clerk who poked his head in at the door; nevertheless he got up, exchanged a few words with him, and sat down again. "... In the following cases: physical defect in one of the parties, desertion without communication for five years" — he crooked one short hair-covered finger — "adultery" (this word he pronounced with evident relish), "subdivided as follows" (he continued crooking his plump fingers, though plainly the three cases and their subdivisions could not really be put on the same footing): "physical defect of the husband or of the wife, adultery of the husband or of the wife." Since by now he had used up all his fingers, he straightened them out again and went on: "That is the theory; but I imagine you have done me the honor of coming to me to find out how it works in practice. Therefore, going on precedent, I must tell you that in practice every divorce case can be reduced to the following — no physical defect, I take it, and no desertion either?..."
Alexey Alexandrovitch bowed his head in agreement.

"— reduces, then, to this: adultery on the part of one spouse, and detection of the guilty party in the act, either by mutual arrangement or, failing such arrangement, by accident. It must be said that the second of those is rarely seen in practice," the lawyer remarked, and shooting a glance at Alexey Alexandrovitch, paused — like a man selling pistols who has finished praising each one and is now waiting for the customer to choose. But Alexey Alexandrovitch said nothing, so the lawyer continued: "The most usual and straightforward course — the sensible one, in my view — is adultery by mutual consent. I would not allow myself to put it that way to an uneducated client," he said, "but I assume you take my meaning."
Alexey Alexandrovitch was so shaken, however, that he did not at once grasp the good sense of adultery by mutual consent, and his eyes betrayed his confusion; the lawyer was quick to assist him.

"People cannot go on living together — that is the fact. And if both of them agree on the point, the details and formalities don't matter much. At the same time it is the simplest and most reliable method."
Alexey Alexandrovitch now understood completely. But he had religious scruples that stood in the way of such a plan.
"That is out of the question in my case," he said. "Only one option remains: accidental detection, supported by letters which I have in my possession."
At the mention of letters the lawyer pursed his lips and produced a thin little sound of compassion and contempt.

"Consider, please," he began, "that cases of that sort, as you know, fall under ecclesiastical jurisdiction; the reverend fathers are fond of going into the smallest details in such cases," he said with a smile that revealed his sympathy with the reverend fathers' taste. "Letters may, of course, provide partial confirmation; but the detection must be of the most direct kind — that is, by eyewitnesses. In fact, if you do me the honor of placing your confidence in me, you will do well to leave the choice of methods to me. If you want the result, you must accept the means."
"If that is so...." Alexey Alexandrovitch began, suddenly going pale; but at that moment the lawyer got up and went to the door again to deal with the intruding clerk.
"Tell her we don't haggle over our fees!" he said, and came back to Alexey Alexandrovitch.
On his way back he caught yet another moth without being noticed. "My rep curtains will be in a fine state by the summer!" he thought, frowning.
"You were saying?..." he prompted.

"I will let you know my decision by letter," Alexey Alexandrovitch said, standing up and gripping the table. He stood for a moment in silence, then said: "From what you have told me I may, therefore, conclude that a divorce can be obtained? I would ask you to let me know your terms."

"It can be obtained if you give me complete freedom of action," the lawyer answered, ignoring his question. "When may I expect to hear from you?" he asked, moving toward the door, his eyes and his polished boots gleaming.
"In a week. Please be so kind as to send me your reply as to whether you will take the case, and on what terms."
"Very good."

The lawyer bowed respectfully, saw his client out, and, left alone, gave himself up to his amusement. He felt so cheerful that, against his usual rules, he made a reduction in his terms for the haggling lady, and gave up catching moths, having decided once and for all that next winter he must have the furniture reupholstered in velvet, like Sigonin's.

title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: Alexey Alexandrovitch had won a brilliant victory at the session of the Commission of August 17th, but in the aftermath that victory cut the ground out from under him. The new commission for the inquiry into the condition of the native tribes in every aspect had been formed and dispatched to its destination with an uncommon speed and energy that came from Alexey Alexandrovitch himself. Within three months a report was delivered. The condition of the native tribes had been examined in its political, administrative, economic, ethnographic, material, and religious aspects. To every one of these questions the report offered admirably stated answers, answers admitting no shade of doubt — for they were not the product of human thought, which is always liable to error, but the product of official activity. All of them rested on official data supplied by governors and heads of churches, founded on the reports of district magistrates and ecclesiastical superintendents, founded in turn on the reports of parochial overseers and parish priests; so every answer was unhesitating and certain. Questions such as why crops fail, why certain tribes cling to their ancient beliefs, and so on — questions which, without the convenient intervention of the official machinery, are not and cannot be settled for ages — received full, confident solutions. And those solutions all favored Alexey Alexandrovitch's contention. But Stremov, stung to the quick at the last session, had, on receipt of the commission's report, resorted to a tactic Alexey Alexandrovitch had not foreseen. Stremov, bringing several members along with him, crossed over to Alexey Alexandrovitch's side, and not content with warmly defending the measure Karenin had proposed, put forward other, more extreme measures in the same direction. These measures, exaggerated still further beyond Alexey Alexandrovitch's original idea, were passed by the commission — and then Stremov's strategy became clear. Pushed to the extreme, the measures suddenly looked so absurd that the highest authorities, public opinion, intellectual ladies, and the newspapers all at once turned on them, expressing their indignation both with the measures and with their nominal author, Alexey Alexandrovitch. Stremov drew back, pretending he had simply followed Karenin's lead and was now astonished and distressed at the result. That meant Alexey Alexandrovitch's defeat. But despite his failing health, despite his domestic troubles, he did not give in. The commission split. Some members, headed by Stremov, justified their mistake by saying they had put their trust in the revising commission Alexey Alexandrovitch had set up, and now declared the commission's report worthless — so much waste paper. Alexey Alexandrovitch, with a following of those who saw the danger of so revolutionary an attitude toward official documents, kept defending the statements obtained by the revising commission. As a result, in the upper spheres — and even in society at large — everything was in confusion, and although everyone was interested, no one could say whether the native tribes really were sinking into poverty and ruin or whether they were thriving. Alexey Alexandrovitch's position, partly because of this and partly because of the contempt heaped on him for his wife's infidelity, became very precarious. And in this position he took an important decision. To the astonishment of the commission, he announced that he would request permission to go and investigate the question himself, on the spot. Having obtained permission, Alexey Alexandrovitch prepared to set out for those distant provinces.
Alexey Alexandrovitch's departure made a great stir, all the more because just before leaving he officially returned the posting fares allotted to him for twelve horses to drive to his destination.
"I think it very noble," Betsy said about it to Princess Myakaya. "Why take money for posting horses when everyone knows there are railways everywhere now?"
But Princess Myakaya disagreed, and Princess Tverskaya's opinion in fact irritated her.

"It's all very well for you to talk," she said, "when you have I don't know how many millions; but I'm always glad when my husband goes off on a revising tour in the summer. It's good for him, pleasant traveling about, and we have a settled arrangement that I keep a carriage and coachman on the money."
On the way to the distant provinces, Alexey Alexandrovitch stopped for three days in Moscow.

The day after he arrived he was driving back from a call on the governor-general. At the crossroads by Gazetny Place, where there are always crowds of carriages and sledges, Alexey Alexandrovitch suddenly heard his name called out in such a loud, cheerful voice that he could not help looking round. At the corner of the pavement, in a short, stylish overcoat and a low-crowned fashionable hat tipped jauntily to one side, with a smile that flashed white teeth and red lips, stood Stepan Arkadyevitch — radiant, young, and beaming. He called out to him insistently, refusing to let him pass without stopping. One arm rested on the window of a carriage halted at the corner, and out of the window leaned the heads of a lady in a velvet hat and two children. Stepan Arkadyevitch was smiling and waving his brother-in-law over. The lady gave a kindly smile too and also waved her hand to Alexey Alexandrovitch. It was Dolly with her children.

Alexey Alexandrovitch had no wish to see anyone in Moscow, and least of all his wife's brother. He raised his hat and would have driven on, but Stepan Arkadyevitch told his coachman to stop and ran across the snow to him.

"Well, what a shame not to let us know! Been here long? I was at Dussot's yesterday and saw 'Karenin' on the guest list, but it never occurred to me it was you," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, sticking his head in at the carriage window, "or I'd have looked you up. I am glad to see you!" he added, knocking one foot against the other to shake off the snow. "Shame on you for not letting us know!" he repeated.
"I had no time; I am very busy," Alexey Alexandrovitch answered dryly.
"Come over to my wife — she so wants to see you."
Alexey Alexandrovitch unfolded the rug wrapped around his frozen feet, climbed out of the carriage, and crossed the snow to Darya Alexandrovna.
"Why, Alexey Alexandrovitch, why are you cutting us like this?" Dolly said, smiling.
"I have been very busy. Delighted to see you!" he said in a tone that made plain how annoyed he was by the encounter. "How are you?"
"Tell me, how is my darling Anna?"
Alexey Alexandrovitch mumbled something and would have moved off, but Stepan Arkadyevitch stopped him.
"I'll tell you what we'll do tomorrow. Dolly, ask him to dinner. We'll invite Koznishev and Pestsov, so he can have a taste of our Moscow celebrities."
"Yes, please, do come," Dolly said; "we'll be expecting you at five, or six o'clock if you prefer. How is my darling Anna? It's been so long...."
"She is quite well," Alexey Alexandrovitch mumbled, frowning. "Delighted!" — and he moved off toward his carriage.
"You'll come?" Dolly called after him.
Alexey Alexandrovitch said something Dolly could not catch over the noise of the moving carriages.
"I'll come round tomorrow!" Stepan Arkadyevitch shouted after him.
Alexey Alexandrovitch climbed into his carriage and buried himself inside it so as neither to see nor to be seen.

"Queer fish!" Stepan Arkadyevitch said to his wife, and glancing at his watch, he made a sweep of his hand before his face — a caress to his wife and children — and strolled jauntily along the pavement.
"Stiva! Stiva!" Dolly called, reddening.
He turned round.
"I need to buy coats, you know, for Grisha and Tanya. Give me the money."
"Never mind — tell them I'll pay the bill!" — and off he went, nodding genially to an acquaintance who drove by.

title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: The next day was Sunday. Stepan Arkadyevitch went to the Grand Theater for a ballet rehearsal and gave Masha Tchibisova, a pretty little dancer he had just taken under his protection, the coral necklace he had promised her the night before; in the dim daylight backstage he also managed to kiss her pretty little face, which was radiant over the gift. Besides giving her the necklace, he wanted to arrange a meeting after the ballet. He explained that he could not come at the start of the performance but promised to be there for the last act and take her to supper. From the theater Stepan Arkadyevitch drove to Ohotny Row, picked out the fish and asparagus for dinner himself, and by noon was at Dussot's, where he had three people to see — luckily all staying at the same hotel: Levin, just back from abroad and lodging there; the new head of his department, who had just been promoted to that position and had come to Moscow on a tour of inspection; and his brother-in-law Karenin, whom he had to see in order to be sure of getting him to dinner.

Stepan Arkadyevitch enjoyed dining out, but he liked even better to host a dinner — small but very select, both in the food and drink and in the choice of guests. He was especially pleased with that day's program. There would be fresh perch, asparagus, and — _la pièce de resistance_ — first-rate but plain roast beef, with wines to match: that was for the eating and drinking. Kitty and Levin would be there, and so that this would not be too obvious, there would be a girl cousin too, and young Shtcherbatsky, and — _la pièce de resistance_ among the guests — Sergey Koznishev and Alexey Alexandrovitch. Sergey Ivanovitch was a Moscow man and a philosopher; Alexey Alexandrovitch a Petersburger and a practical statesman. He had also invited the well-known eccentric enthusiast Pestsov — a liberal, a great talker, a musician, a historian, and the most charmingly youthful man of fifty you could meet — who would serve as a sauce or garnish for Koznishev and Karenin. He would needle them and set them off.

The second installment for the forest had come in from the merchant and was not yet spent; Dolly had been very pleasant and good-natured of late; and the prospect of the dinner pleased Stepan Arkadyevitch from every angle. He was in the lightest of moods. There were two slightly unpleasant things, but they were drowned in the sea of good-humored gaiety that flooded Stepan Arkadyevitch's soul. The first was that when he had met Alexey Alexandrovitch on the street the day before, he had noticed how cold and reserved his brother-in-law was with him, and putting the expression on Alexey Alexandrovitch's face, and the fact that he had not come to see them or even let them know of his arrival, together with the rumors he had heard about Anna and Vronsky, Stepan Arkadyevitch guessed that something was wrong between the husband and wife.

That was one disagreeable item. The other slightly disagreeable item was that the new head of his department, like all new heads, already had the reputation of being a terror — a man who got up at six in the morning, worked like a horse, and demanded that his subordinates do the same. On top of that, this new chief had a name for being a bear in his manners, and was, by all accounts, a man of the kind exactly opposite to that of his predecessor, the type Stepan Arkadyevitch himself had belonged to up to now. The day before, Stepan Arkadyevitch had appeared at the office in uniform, and the new chief had been very affable and had talked with him as with an old acquaintance. So Stepan Arkadyevitch felt it was his duty to call on him in plain clothes. The thought that the new chief might not give him a warm welcome was the other unpleasant point. But Stepan Arkadyevitch felt instinctively that everything would _come round_ all right. "They're all people, all men, like the rest of us poor sinners — why be nasty and quarrelsome?" he thought as he walked into the hotel.

"Good day, Vassily," he said, going down the corridor with his hat tipped to one side and addressing a footman he knew; "why, you've let your whiskers grow! Levin, number seven, right? Take me up, please. And find out whether Count Anitchkin" — this was the new chief — "is receiving."
"Yes, sir," Vassily answered, smiling. "You've not been to see us for a long while."
"I was here yesterday, but at the other entrance. Is this number seven?"
Levin was standing in the middle of the room with a peasant from Tver, measuring out a fresh bearskin, when Stepan Arkadyevitch walked in.
"What! you killed him?" Stepan Arkadyevitch cried. "Well done! A she-bear? How are you, Arhip!"
He shook hands with the peasant and sat down on the edge of a chair without taking off his coat and hat.
"Come now, take off your coat and stay a little," said Levin, taking his hat.

"No, I haven't time; I only looked in for a moment," Stepan Arkadyevitch answered. He unbuttoned his coat, but ended up taking it off after all, and sat for a whole hour talking with Levin about hunting and the most personal subjects.
"Come on, tell me, what did you do abroad? Where have you been?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked once the peasant had gone.
"Oh, I was in Germany, in Prussia, in France, and in England — not in the capitals, but in the manufacturing towns — and saw a great deal that was new to me. I'm glad I went."
"Yes, I know your idea about how to solve the labor question."

"Not at all: in Russia there can be no labor question. In Russia the question is the relation of the working people to the land; the labor question exists there too — but there it's a matter of repairing what's been ruined, while with us...."
Stepan Arkadyevitch listened to Levin attentively.

"Yes, yes!" he said. "It's very possible you're right. But I'm glad you're in good spirits, hunting bears, working, taking an interest in things. Shtcherbatsky told me another story — he met you somewhere — that you were in such a depressed state, talking of nothing but death...."

"Well, what of it? I haven't given up thinking of death," Levin said. "It's true that it's high time I was dead, and that all this is nonsense. I'm telling you the truth. I really do value my idea and my work; but in reality just consider this: our whole world is nothing but a speck of mildew that has grown up on a tiny planet. And for us to suppose we can have anything great — ideas, work — it's all dust and ashes."
"But all that's as old as the hills, my boy!"

"It is old, but you know, once you really take it in, then somehow everything becomes meaningless. Once you grasp that you'll die tomorrow if not today, and nothing will be left, then everything is so trivial! I think my idea is very important, but it turns out to be just as trivial, even if it were carried out, as that bear-killing business. So one goes on living — amusing oneself with hunting, with work — anything to avoid thinking of death!"
Stepan Arkadyevitch smiled a subtle, affectionate smile as he listened to Levin.
"Well, of course! Now you've come round to my point of view. Remember how you used to attack me for chasing enjoyment in life? Don't be so hard on us, O moralist!"
"No; all the same, what's fine in life is...." Levin hesitated — "oh, I don't know. All I know is that we'll soon be dead."
"Why so soon?"
"And you know, life has less charm once you think of death — but more peace."
"On the contrary, the end is always the best part. But I really must go," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, getting up for the tenth time.
"Oh, no, stay a little longer!" Levin said, holding him back. "When will we see each other again? I leave tomorrow."
"What an idiot I am! That's exactly what I came for! You absolutely must come to dinner with us today. Your brother is coming, and Karenin, my brother-in-law."

"You don't mean to say he's here?" Levin said, and was on the point of asking about Kitty. He had heard at the start of the winter that she was in Petersburg with her sister, the diplomat's wife, and he did not know whether she had come back; but he changed his mind and did not ask. "Whether she's coming or not, I don't care," he told himself.
"So you'll come?"
"Of course."
"Five o'clock, then, and no evening dress."

And Stepan Arkadyevitch got up and went downstairs to see the new head of his department. His instinct had not misled him. The terrifying new chief turned out to be an extremely agreeable man, and Stepan Arkadyevitch had lunch with him and stayed on, so that it was four o'clock by the time he got to Alexey Alexandrovitch.

title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Coming back from church service, Alexey Alexandrovitch had spent the whole morning indoors. He had two pieces of business to deal with: first, to receive and send on a deputation from the native tribes that was on its way to Petersburg and was now in Moscow; second, to write the promised letter to the lawyer. The deputation, although it had been summoned at Alexey Alexandrovitch's instigation, had its uncomfortable, even dangerous side, and he was glad he had found it in Moscow. Its members had not the faintest grasp of their duty or the part they were meant to play. They naively believed it was their job to set out their needs and the actual conditions on the ground before the commission and to ask the government for help, and quite failed to grasp that some of their statements and requests supported the opposing side's case and so spoiled the whole business. Alexey Alexandrovitch worked with them at length, drew up a program from which they were not to depart, and after sending them off wrote a letter to Petersburg to guide the deputation there. His chief ally in the affair was Countess Lidia Ivanovna. She was a specialist in deputations, and no one knew better than she did how to manage them and steer them in the right direction. Having finished with that, Alexey Alexandrovitch wrote the letter to the lawyer. Without the slightest hesitation he gave him a free hand to act as he thought best. With the letter he enclosed three of Vronsky's notes to Anna, which he had taken from her portfolio.

Ever since Alexey Alexandrovitch had left home meaning never to return to his family, and since he had been to the lawyer's and spoken about his intention, if only to one man, and especially since he had transferred the matter from real life into the world of ink and paper, he had grown more and more accustomed to his decision, and could now clearly see how it was to be carried out.
He was sealing the envelope to the lawyer when he heard Stepan Arkadyevitch's loud voice. Stepan Arkadyevitch was arguing with Alexey Alexandrovitch's servant and insisting on being announced.
"No matter," Alexey Alexandrovitch thought, "so much the better. I'll tell him at once where I stand with regard to his sister, and explain why I can't dine with him."
"Show him in!" he said aloud, gathering up his papers and tucking them into the blotter.

"There, you see — you're talking nonsense, and he's at home!" came Stepan Arkadyevitch's voice, addressed to the servant who had refused to let him in; pulling off his coat as he came, Oblonsky walked into the room. "Well, I'm awfully glad I've caught you! So I trust...." Stepan Arkadyevitch began cheerfully.
"I cannot come," Alexey Alexandrovitch said coldly, standing and not asking his visitor to sit down.

Alexey Alexandrovitch had meant to step at once into those frigid relations he ought to maintain with the brother of a wife against whom he was bringing a divorce suit. But he had not reckoned with the ocean of kindliness brimming in Stepan Arkadyevitch's heart.
Stepan Arkadyevitch's clear, shining eyes opened wide.
"Why can't you? What do you mean?" he asked, bewildered, in French. "Oh, but it's a promise. And we're all counting on you."
"I want to tell you that I cannot dine at your house, because the relationship that has existed between us must end."
"How? What do you mean? What for?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling.
"Because I am beginning a divorce suit against your sister, my wife. I should have...."
But before Alexey Alexandrovitch could finish his sentence, Stepan Arkadyevitch behaved in a way he had not at all expected. He groaned and sank into an armchair.
"No, Alexey Alexandrovitch! What are you saying?" Oblonsky cried, and the pain showed in his face.
"It is so."
"Forgive me, I can't, I can't believe it!"

Alexey Alexandrovitch sat down, sensing that his words had not had the effect he expected, and that he would have to explain his position, and that no matter what he said, his relationship with his brother-in-law would not really change.
"Yes, I have been driven to the painful necessity of seeking a divorce," he said.

"I will say just one thing, Alexey Alexandrovitch. I know you to be an excellent, upright man; I know Anna — forgive me, I cannot change my opinion of her — to be a good, an excellent woman; and so, forgive me, I cannot believe it. There must be some misunderstanding," he said.
"Oh, if it were only a misunderstanding!..."
"Pardon, I understand," Stepan Arkadyevitch broke in. "But of course.... One thing: you must not act in haste. You must not, you must not act in haste!"
"I am not acting in haste," Alexey Alexandrovitch said coldly, "but one cannot ask anyone for advice in such a matter. I have made up my mind completely."

"This is awful!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "There is one thing I would beg you to do, Alexey Alexandrovitch. I beseech you, do it!" he said. "No action has been taken yet, if I understand rightly. Before you go to your lawyer, see my wife, talk to her. She loves Anna like a sister, she loves you, and she's a wonderful woman. For God's sake, talk with her! Do me that favor, I beg you!"
Alexey Alexandrovitch thought, and Stepan Arkadyevitch watched him sympathetically, not breaking his silence.
"You will go and see her?"
"I don't know. That's just why I haven't been over. I think our relations must change."

"Why should they? I don't see it. Allow me to think that, apart from our family connection, you have for me, at least in part, the same friendly feeling I have always had for you ... and a sincere respect," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, pressing his hand. "Even if your worst suspicions were correct, I don't — and never would — take it upon myself to judge either side, and I see no reason why our relations should suffer. But now, do this — come and see my wife."
"Well, we see the matter differently," Alexey Alexandrovitch said coldly. "However, we won't go into it."

"No; why shouldn't you come to dinner today anyway? My wife is expecting you. Please, do come. And above all, talk it over with her. She's a wonderful woman. For God's sake, on my knees, I implore you!"
"If you wish it so much, I'll come," said Alexey Alexandrovitch with a sigh.

And, eager to change the subject, he asked about something that interested them both — the new head of Stepan Arkadyevitch's department, a man not yet old, who had suddenly been promoted to such a high position.

Alexey Alexandrovitch had never cared for Count Anitchkin and had always disagreed with him on policy. But now, from a feeling familiar enough among officials — the hatred a man passed over for promotion feels for the one promoted ahead of him — he could not stand him.
"Well, have you seen him?" said Alexey Alexandrovitch with a malicious smile.
"Of course; he was at our meeting yesterday. He seems to know his job thoroughly and to be very energetic."

"Yes, but what is his energy aimed at?" Alexey Alexandrovitch said. "Is he trying to accomplish anything, or only to undo what's been done? It's the great misfortune of our government — this paper administration of which he is a worthy representative."

"Really, I don't know what fault one could find with him. I don't know his policies, but one thing I do know — he's a very nice fellow," Stepan Arkadyevitch said. "I've just been with him, and he really is a capital fellow. We lunched together, and I taught him how to make — you know that drink, wine and oranges. It's so cooling. It's amazing he didn't know it. He took to it like anything. No, really, he's a capital fellow."
Stepan Arkadyevitch glanced at his watch.
"Why, good heavens, it's already four, and I still have to call on Dolgovushin! So please do come round for dinner. You can't imagine how you will hurt my wife and me."
The way Alexey Alexandrovitch saw his brother-in-law out was very different from the way he had received him.
"I've promised, and I'll come," he answered wearily.
"Believe me, I appreciate it, and I hope you won't regret it," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, smiling.
And, pulling on his coat as he went, he patted the footman on the head, chuckled, and went out.
"Five o'clock, and not evening dress, please!" he shouted once more, turning at the door.

title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: It was past five, and several guests had already arrived before the host himself came home. He walked in together with Sergey Ivanovitch Koznishev and Pestsov, who had reached the front door at the same moment. These were the two leading representatives of the Moscow intellectuals, as Oblonsky had called them. Both were men respected for their character and their intelligence. They respected each other but were in complete and hopeless disagreement on almost every subject — not because they belonged to opposing parties, but precisely because they belonged to the same party (their enemies refused to see any distinction between their views); only, within that party, each had his own particular shade of opinion. And since no difference is harder to bridge than a difference of opinion about semi-abstract questions, they never agreed on anything, and had long since grown used to laughing without rancor at each other's incorrigible aberrations.

They were just going in at the door, talking about the weather, when Stepan Arkadyevitch caught up with them. In the drawing room already were Prince Alexander Dmitrievitch Shtcherbatsky, young Shtcherbatsky, Turovtsin, Kitty, and Karenin.

Stepan Arkadyevitch saw at once that things were not going well in the drawing room without him. Darya Alexandrovna, in her best gray silk gown, plainly worried about the children, who were to dine on their own in the nursery, and about her husband's absence, was not equal to the job of getting the party to mix without him. They were all sitting like so many priests' wives on a visit (as the old prince put it), obviously wondering what they were doing there and pumping out remarks just to keep the silence at bay. Turovtsin — good, simple soul — felt unmistakably like a fish out of water, and the smile his thick lips offered Stepan Arkadyevitch said, as plainly as any words: "Well, old boy, you've planted me in a learned set! A drinking party now, or the _Château des Fleurs_, would be more my line!" The old prince sat in silence, his bright little eyes watching Karenin from the side, and Stepan Arkadyevitch saw that he had already worked up some phrase to sum up that politician whom the guests had been invited to consume as though he were a sturgeon. Kitty kept looking at the door, mustering all her strength to keep from blushing when Konstantin Levin came in. Young Shtcherbatsky, who had not been introduced to Karenin, was trying to look as if he were not in the least aware of the fact. Karenin himself, following the Petersburg fashion for a dinner with ladies, was wearing evening dress and a white tie. Stepan Arkadyevitch could tell from his face that he had come only to keep his promise, and that being present at this gathering was a disagreeable duty. He was, in fact, the main cause of the chill that had numbed all the guests before Stepan Arkadyevitch came in.

Entering the drawing room, Stepan Arkadyevitch apologized, explaining that he had been held up by that prince — the standard scapegoat for all his absences and tardiness — and in a single moment he had everyone acquainted with everyone else; pairing Alexey Alexandrovitch with Sergey Koznishev, he launched them into a discussion on the Russification of Poland, into which Pestsov immediately plunged with them. Slapping Turovtsin on the shoulder, he whispered something amusing in his ear and parked him beside his wife and the old prince. Then he told Kitty she was looking very pretty that evening, and introduced Shtcherbatsky to Karenin. In a moment he had kneaded the social dough so well that the drawing room came alive, and there was a merry buzz of voices. The only person not yet there was Konstantin Levin. So much the better, since on going into the dining room Stepan Arkadyevitch discovered, to his horror, that the port and sherry had come from Depré's and not from Levy's; sending the coachman off to Levy's as fast as possible, he was about to head back into the drawing room.
In the dining room he ran into Konstantin Levin.
"I'm not late?"
"You can never help being late!" Stepan Arkadyevitch said, taking him by the arm.
"Have you got many people? Who's here?" Levin asked, unable to keep from blushing, as he knocked the snow off his cap with his glove.
"All our own set. Kitty's here. Come along, I'll introduce you to Karenin."

Stepan Arkadyevitch, despite his liberal views, knew very well that to be presented to Karenin was sure to be considered a flattering distinction, and so served the honor up to his best friends. But at that instant Konstantin Levin was in no state to appreciate such an introduction. He had not seen Kitty since that memorable evening when he had run into Vronsky — not counting, that is, the brief glimpse he had had of her on the highroad. At the bottom of his heart he had known he would see her here tonight. But to keep his thoughts free of it, he had tried to convince himself that he did not know. Now, hearing that she was here, he was suddenly aware of such joy and at the same time of such dread that his breath caught and he could not bring out what he wanted to say.
"What is she like, what is she like? Like she used to be, or like she was in the carriage? What if Darya Alexandrovna told the truth? Why shouldn't it be the truth?" he thought.
"Oh, please, introduce me to Karenin," he got out with an effort, and with a step of desperate resolution walked into the drawing room and saw her.
She was not as she had been before, nor as she had been in the carriage; she was quite different.

She was frightened, shy, abashed — and even more enchanting for it. She saw him the moment he came into the room. She had been waiting for him. She was overjoyed, and so flustered by her own joy that there was a moment — when he went over to her sister and looked at her again — when she, and he, and Dolly, who saw it all, thought she would crack and burst into tears. She flushed, turned pale, flushed again, and grew faint, her lips quivering as she waited for him to come over. He went up to her, bowed, and held out his hand without speaking. Apart from the slight tremor of her lips and the moisture in her eyes that made them brighter, her smile was almost calm as she said:
"How long it has been since we've seen each other!" — and with a desperate effort she pressed his hand with her own cold one.
"You haven't seen me, but I have seen you," Levin said, with a smile that beamed with happiness. "I saw you when you were driving from the railway station to Ergushovo."
"When?" she asked, surprised.

"You were on your way to Ergushovo," Levin said, feeling as though he might sob from the rapture flooding his heart. "And how could I dare let any unworthy thought enter my head about this touching creature? And, yes, I do believe what Darya Alexandrovna told me is true," he thought.
Stepan Arkadyevitch took his arm and led him over to Karenin.
"Let me introduce you." He gave their names.
"Very glad to meet you again," Alexey Alexandrovitch said coldly, shaking Levin's hand.
"You know each other?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked, surprised.
"We spent three hours together on the train," Levin said with a smile, "but came out, as in a masquerade, quite mystified — at least I was."
"Nonsense! Come along, please," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, gesturing toward the dining room.

The men went into the dining room and stepped up to a table set with six kinds of spirits and as many cheeses, some with little silver spades and some without, caviar, herrings, preserves of various sorts, and plates of sliced French bread.
The men stood around the pungent spirits and salty hors d'oeuvres, and the discussion about the Russification of Poland between Koznishev, Karenin, and Pestsov died down in anticipation of dinner.
Sergey Ivanovitch had no equal at winding up the most heated and serious argument with some unexpected pinch of Attic salt that shifted his opponent's mood. He did so now.
Alexey Alexandrovitch had been arguing that the Russification of Poland could only be brought about as a consequence of larger measures, which the Russian government ought to introduce.
Pestsov maintained that one nation can only absorb another when it has the denser population.
Koznishev granted both points, but with reservations. As they were leaving the drawing room to round off the argument, Koznishev said with a smile:

"So, then, for the Russification of our foreign populations there is only one method — to have as many children as one can. My brother and I are terribly in default, I see. You married men, especially you, Stepan Arkadyevitch, are the real patriots — what number have you got up to?" he said, smiling genially at his host and holding out a tiny wineglass.
Everyone laughed, and Stepan Arkadyevitch most heartily of all.
"Oh, yes, that's the best method!" he said, munching cheese and filling the wineglass with a special spirit. The conversation broke off at the joke.

"This cheese isn't bad. Shall I give you some?" said the master of the house. "Why, have you been going in for gymnastics again?" he asked Levin, pinching his muscle with his left hand. Levin smiled, flexed his arm, and under Stepan Arkadyevitch's fingers the muscle swelled up like a sound cheese, hard as a knob of iron, through the fine cloth of his coat.
"What biceps! A regular Samson!"

"I imagine bear-hunting takes great strength," remarked Alexey Alexandrovitch, who had only the haziest notion of the chase. He cut off and spread with cheese a wafer of bread as fine as a spider's web.
Levin smiled.
"Not at all. Quite the contrary — a child can kill a bear," he said, with a slight bow as he stepped aside for the ladies, who were approaching the table.

"I hear you killed a bear!" said Kitty, trying conscientiously to spear with her fork a perverse mushroom that kept sliding away, and setting the lace quivering over her white arm. "Are there bears on your place?" she added, turning her charming little head to him and smiling.

There was apparently nothing extraordinary in what she said, but what unspoken meaning every sound, every turn of her lips, her eyes, her hand had for him as she said it! There was a plea for forgiveness, and trust in him, and tenderness — soft, timid tenderness — and promise and hope and love for him, all of which he could not help believing, and which choked him with happiness.
"No, we were hunting in Tver province. Coming back from there I met your _beau-frère_ on the train, or rather your _beau-frère_'s brother-in-law," he said with a smile. "It was an amusing meeting."
And he began telling, with droll good humor, how, after not sleeping all night, in an old long-skirted fur-lined coat, he had got into Alexey Alexandrovitch's compartment.

"The conductor, forgetting the proverb, would have thrown me out on account of my clothes; but then I started expressing my feelings in elevated language, and ... you, too," he said, turning to Karenin and forgetting his name, "at first would have evicted me on the grounds of the old coat, but afterwards took my side, for which I am extremely grateful."
"The right of passengers to choose their seats is too poorly defined in general," Alexey Alexandrovitch said, wiping the tips of his fingers on his handkerchief.

"I could see you were uncertain about me," said Levin, smiling good-naturedly, "but I made a point of plunging into intellectual conversation to compensate for the defects of my dress." Sergey Ivanovitch, while keeping up a conversation with their hostess, had one ear cocked toward his brother and shot a sidelong glance at him. "What's gotten into him today? Why this conquering-hero air?" he thought. He did not know that Levin felt as though he had grown wings. Levin knew she was listening to his words and was glad to listen to him. And that was the only thing that interested him. Not just in that room, but in the whole world, there existed for him only himself — with enormously increased importance and dignity in his own eyes — and her. He felt himself on a pinnacle that made him dizzy, and far down below were all those nice, excellent Karenins, Oblonskys, and all the rest of the world.
Quite without drawing attention to it, without so much as a glance at them, as though there were no other places left, Stepan Arkadyevitch seated Levin and Kitty side by side.
"Oh, you may as well sit there," he said to Levin.

The dinner was as choice as the china, of which Stepan Arkadyevitch was a connoisseur. The _soupe Marie-Louise_ was a splendid success; the tiny pies eaten with it melted in the mouth and were beyond reproach. The two footmen and Matvey, in white cravats, handled the dishes and wines unobtrusively, quietly, and quickly. On the material side the dinner was a success; on the immaterial side, no less so. The conversation, sometimes general, sometimes between individuals, never flagged, and toward the end the company grew so lively that the men rose from the table without breaking off their talk, and even Alexey Alexandrovitch thawed.

title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: Pestsov liked to thrash an argument out to the end and was not satisfied with Sergey Ivanovitch's remark, all the more because he felt the unfairness of his view.
"I didn't mean," he said over the soup, addressing Alexey Alexandrovitch, "density of population by itself, but in combination with fundamental ideas, and not by means of principles alone."

"It seems to me," Alexey Alexandrovitch said languidly and without haste, "that those come to the same thing. In my opinion, influence over another people is possible only to the people at the higher level of development, which...."

"But that's the very question," Pestsov broke in in his bass. He was always in a hurry to speak and always seemed to put his whole soul into what he was saying. "What are we to make this higher development consist in? The English, the French, the Germans — which of them stands at the highest stage? Which of them will nationalize the other? We see the Rhine provinces turned French — yet the Germans aren't at a lower stage!" he shouted. "There's another law at work in such cases."
"It seems to me that the greater influence is always on the side of true civilization," said Alexey Alexandrovitch, lifting his eyebrows a little.
"But what are we to take as the outward signs of true civilization?" said Pestsov.
"I imagine such signs are generally well known," Alexey Alexandrovitch said.

"Are they really fully known?" Sergey Ivanovitch cut in with a subtle smile. "The current view is that genuine culture must be purely classical; but we see violent disputes on each side of the question, and there's no denying that the opposite camp has strong points in its favor."
"You're for the classics, Sergey Ivanovitch. Will you take red wine?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch.

"I am not expressing my own view of either form of culture," Sergey Ivanovitch said, holding out his glass with a condescending smile, as though to a child. "I am only saying that both sides have strong arguments to support them," he went on, turning to Alexey Alexandrovitch. "My sympathies, by training, are classical; but in this debate I personally cannot reach a conclusion. I see no decisive grounds for giving classical studies priority over scientific ones."
"The natural sciences have just as much educational value," put in Pestsov. "Take astronomy, take botany, or zoology with its system of general principles."

"I can't quite agree with that," answered Alexey Alexandrovitch. "It seems to me one must concede that the very process of studying the forms of language has a uniquely beneficial effect on intellectual development. Moreover, it cannot be denied that the influence of the classical authors is in the highest degree moral, while, unfortunately, with the study of the natural sciences are associated the false and pernicious doctrines that are the curse of our day."
