Sergey Ivanovitch would have said something, but Pestsov broke in with his rich bass. He went at the rightness of Alexey Alexandrovitch's view warmly. Sergey Ivanovitch waited serenely for his turn, plainly with a crushing reply ready.

"But," said Sergey Ivanovitch with a subtle smile, addressing Karenin, "one must allow that weighing all the pros and cons of classical and scientific studies is a difficult task, and the question which form of education was to be preferred would not have been decided so quickly and conclusively if there had not been, in favor of classical education, as you put it just now, its moral — _disons le mot_ — anti-nihilist influence."
"No doubt."

"If it weren't for the special anti-nihilist property of classical studies, we'd have given more thought to the subject and weighed the arguments on both sides," Sergey Ivanovitch went on with a subtle smile; "we'd have given room for both tendencies. But now we know these little pills of classical learning possess the medicinal property of anti-nihilism, and we boldly prescribe them to our patients.... But what if they had no such medicinal property?" he wound up, smiling.

At Sergey Ivanovitch's little pills everyone laughed; Turovtsin especially roared in jolly delight, glad at last to have found something to laugh at — which was all he ever looked for when listening to conversation.

Stepan Arkadyevitch had not been wrong to invite Pestsov. With Pestsov around, intellectual conversation never flagged for an instant. The moment Sergey Ivanovitch had wrapped up the previous topic with his joke, Pestsov launched into a new one.

"I can't even agree," he said, "that the government had any such aim. The government obviously is guided by abstract considerations and remains indifferent to the influence its measures may have. The education of women, for example, would naturally be looked on as likely to be harmful, and yet the government opens schools and universities for women."
And the conversation at once shifted to the new subject of the education of women.
Alexey Alexandrovitch suggested that the education of women tends to be confused with the emancipation of women, and that only on that basis can it be considered dangerous.

"On the contrary, I hold that the two questions are inseparably linked," said Pestsov; "it's a vicious circle. Woman is deprived of rights for lack of education, and the lack of education comes from the absence of rights. We mustn't forget that the subjection of women is so complete, and goes back so many ages, that we are often unwilling to admit the gulf that separates them from us," he said.

"You spoke of rights," said Sergey Ivanovitch, waiting until Pestsov had finished, "meaning the right of serving on juries, of voting, of presiding at official meetings, the right of entering the civil service, of sitting in parliament...."
"No doubt."

"But if women, as a rare exception, can hold such positions, it seems to me you are wrong to use the word 'rights.' It would be more correct to say duties. Every man will agree that in performing the duty of a juror, a witness, a telegraph clerk, we feel we are carrying out duties. And so it would be correct to say that women are seeking duties — and quite legitimately. One can only sympathize with this desire to share in the general work of humanity."
"Quite so," Alexey Alexandrovitch agreed. "The question, I take it, is simply whether they are fit for such duties."
"They will most likely be perfectly fit," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, "when education has become widespread among them. We see this...."

"How about the proverb?" said the old prince, who had been listening to the talk for a while, his little comical eyes twinkling. "I can say it in front of my daughter: her hair is long because her wit is...."
"That's exactly what they thought of the negroes before their emancipation!" Pestsov said angrily.
"What I find strange is that women should seek out fresh duties," Sergey Ivanovitch said, "while we see, unhappily, that men usually try to avoid them."
"Duties are bound up with rights — power, money, honor; those are what women are after," said Pestsov.
"It's as if I demanded the right to be a wet-nurse and felt insulted because women are paid for the work, while no one will take me," said the old prince.
Turovtsin exploded into a loud roar of laughter, and Sergey Ivanovitch was sorry he had not thought of that comparison himself. Even Alexey Alexandrovitch smiled.
"Yes, but a man can't nurse a baby," said Pestsov, "while a woman...."
"No, there was an Englishman who did suckle his child on board ship," the old prince said, feeling at liberty to be free in conversation in front of his own daughters.
"There are about as many such Englishmen as there would be women officials," said Sergey Ivanovitch.
"Yes, but what is a girl to do who has no family?" Stepan Arkadyevitch put in, thinking of Masha Tchibisova, who had been on his mind all along, in agreeing with Pestsov and backing him up.

"If you really looked into the story of such a girl, you'd find she had abandoned a family — her own or a sister's — where she might have found a woman's duties," Darya Alexandrovna unexpectedly broke in with exasperation, probably guessing what sort of girl Stepan Arkadyevitch had in mind.

"But we stand on principle as the ideal," Pestsov replied in his mellow bass. "Woman wants to have rights, to be independent, educated. She is oppressed, humiliated by the awareness of her disadvantages."

"And I'm oppressed and humiliated that they won't engage me at the Foundling," the old prince said again, to the huge delight of Turovtsin, who in his mirth dropped his asparagus thick-end-first into the sauce.

title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: Everyone took part in the conversation except Kitty and Levin. At first, when they were talking about one people influencing another, what Levin had to say on the subject rose in his mind. But those ideas, once so important in his eyes, came into his head now as in a dream and held not the slightest interest for him. It even struck him as strange that they should be so eager to talk about something that was of no use to anyone. Kitty too, one would have thought, should have been interested in what was being said about the rights and education of women. How often she had brooded over the subject, thinking of her friend Varenka abroad and her painful dependence; how often she had wondered what would become of her if she did not marry, and how often she had argued with her sister about it! And yet none of it interested her at all. She and Levin were having a conversation of their own — and yet not a conversation but some kind of mysterious communication that brought them every moment closer and stirred in both of them a sense of joyful terror before the unknown into which they were entering.
At first Levin, answering Kitty's question how he had been able to see her last year in the carriage, told her how he had been walking home from the mowing along the highroad and had met her.

"It was very, very early in the morning. You were probably only just awake. Your mother was asleep in the corner. It was a marvelous morning. I was walking along, wondering who could be in a four-in-hand? It was a splendid team of four with bells, and in a second you flashed past, and I saw you at the window — sitting like this, holding the strings of your cap in both hands, thinking awfully hard about something," he said, smiling. "How I'd love to know what you were thinking about then! Something important?"

"Wasn't I dreadfully untidy?" she wondered, but seeing the smile of ecstasy these recollections called up, she knew that the impression she had made had been very good. She blushed and laughed with delight. "Really, I don't remember."
"How nicely Turovtsin laughs!" said Levin, admiring his moist eyes and shaking chest.
"Have you known him long?" Kitty asked.
"Oh, everyone knows him!"
"And I can see you think he's a horrid man?"
"Not horrid, just empty."

"Oh, you're wrong! And you must give up thinking so right away!" said Kitty. "I used to have a poor opinion of him too, but he, he is an awfully nice and wonderfully good-hearted man. He has a heart of gold."
"How could you find out what sort of heart he has?"

"We are great friends. I know him very well. Last winter, soon after ... you came to see us," she said, with a guilty and at the same time confiding smile, "all of Dolly's children had scarlet fever, and he happened to call on her. And just imagine," she said in a whisper, "he felt so sorry for her that he stayed and started helping her with the children. Yes, and for three weeks he stayed and looked after them like a nurse."
"I'm telling Konstantin Dmitrievitch about Turovtsin in the scarlet fever," she said, leaning toward her sister.

"Yes, it was wonderful, noble!" Dolly said, glancing toward Turovtsin, who had noticed they were talking about him, and smiling gently at him. Levin looked at Turovtsin again and wondered how it was he had not seen the man's goodness before.
"I'm sorry, I'm sorry, and I'll never think ill of people again!" he said merrily, sincerely meaning what he said at that moment.

title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: Bound up with the conversation that had sprung up about the rights of women were certain questions about the inequality of rights in marriage, not suitable to discuss in front of the ladies. Pestsov had touched on them several times during dinner, but Sergey Ivanovitch and Stepan Arkadyevitch had carefully steered him off them.

When they got up from the table and the ladies had left, Pestsov did not follow them, but turned to Alexey Alexandrovitch and began laying out the main grounds of inequality. The inequality in marriage, in his view, lay in the fact that a wife's infidelity and a husband's infidelity were punished unequally, both by the law and by public opinion. Stepan Arkadyevitch hurried up to Alexey Alexandrovitch and offered him a cigar.
"No, I don't smoke," Alexey Alexandrovitch answered calmly, and as though deliberately wanting to show he was not afraid of the subject, he turned to Pestsov with a chilly smile.

"I take it that such a view has a foundation in the very nature of things," he said, and would have gone on into the drawing room. But at that point Turovtsin burst suddenly and unexpectedly into the conversation, addressing Alexey Alexandrovitch.

"You heard, perhaps, about Pryatchnikov?" said Turovtsin, warmed by the champagne he had drunk and long waiting for an opportunity to break the silence weighing on him. "Vasya Pryatchnikov," he said with a good-natured smile on his damp red lips, speaking mainly to the most important guest, Alexey Alexandrovitch, "they told me today he fought a duel with Kvitsky at Tver and killed him."

Just as one always seems to bump one's bruise on a sore spot, so Stepan Arkadyevitch felt now that the conversation, by an unlucky chance, kept landing on Alexey Alexandrovitch's tender place. He would have steered his brother-in-law away again, but Alexey Alexandrovitch himself inquired, with curiosity:
"What did Pryatchnikov fight about?"
"His wife. Acted like a man! Called him out and shot him!"
"Ah!" Alexey Alexandrovitch said indifferently, and, lifting his eyebrows, walked off into the drawing room.
"How glad I am you've come," Dolly said with a frightened smile, meeting him in the outer drawing room. "I have to talk to you. Let's sit here."
Alexey Alexandrovitch, still with the indifferent look his raised eyebrows gave him, sat down beside Darya Alexandrovna and smiled stiffly.
"It's lucky," he said, "especially as I was meaning to ask you to excuse me — I must say good-bye. I have to leave tomorrow."

Darya Alexandrovna was firmly convinced of Anna's innocence, and she felt herself going pale and her lips quivering with anger at this cold, unfeeling man who was so calmly intending to ruin her innocent friend.
"Alexey Alexandrovitch," she said, with desperate resolve looking him in the face, "I asked you about Anna and you made no answer. How is she?"
"She is, I believe, quite well, Darya Alexandrovna," Alexey Alexandrovitch answered, not looking at her.

"Alexey Alexandrovitch, forgive me, I have no right ... but I love Anna like a sister, and I respect her; I beg, I beseech you to tell me what is wrong between you? what is it you find fault with in her?"
Alexey Alexandrovitch frowned and, almost shutting his eyes, lowered his head.

"I assume your husband has told you the grounds on which I consider it necessary to change my attitude to Anna Arkadyevna?" he said, not looking her in the face but eyeing with displeasure Shtcherbatsky, who was walking across the drawing room.

"I don't believe it, I don't believe it, I can't believe it!" Dolly said, clasping her bony hands before her with a forceful gesture. She rose quickly and laid her hand on Alexey Alexandrovitch's sleeve. "We'll be disturbed here. Come this way, please."
Dolly's agitation had an effect on Alexey Alexandrovitch. He got up and submissively followed her into the schoolroom. They sat down at a table covered with an oilcloth slashed by penknives.
"I don't, I don't believe it!" Dolly said, trying to catch his eyes, which kept avoiding hers.
"One can't disbelieve the facts, Darya Alexandrovna," he said, with emphasis on the word "facts."
"But what has she done?" Darya Alexandrovna said. "What exactly has she done?"
"She has abandoned her duty and deceived her husband. That is what she has done," he said.
"No, no, it can't be! No, for God's sake, you are mistaken," Dolly said, pressing her hands to her temples and closing her eyes.

Alexey Alexandrovitch gave a cold smile, with his lips alone, meaning to make clear to her and to himself the firmness of his conviction; but this warm defense, though it could not shake him, reopened his wound. He began to speak with more heat.

"It is extremely difficult to be mistaken when a wife herself informs her husband of the fact — informs him that eight years of her life, and a son, are all a mistake, and that she wants to begin her life over again," he said angrily, with a snort.
"Anna and sin — I can't put them together, I cannot believe it!"

"Darya Alexandrovna," he said, now looking straight into Dolly's kind, troubled face, and feeling his tongue come loose in spite of himself, "I would give a great deal for doubt to be still possible. When I doubted I was wretched, but it was better than it is now. When I doubted I had hope; now there is no hope, and still I doubt everything. I doubt everything so completely that I even hate my son, and sometimes don't believe he's mine. I am very unhappy."
He had not needed to say it. Darya Alexandrovna had seen it the moment he glanced into her face; and she felt sorry for him, and her faith in her friend's innocence began to waver.
"Oh, this is awful, awful! But can it be true that you've decided on a divorce?"
"I have decided on extreme measures. There is nothing else for me to do."
"Nothing else to do, nothing else to do...." she answered, with tears in her eyes. "Oh no, don't say there's nothing else!" she said.

"What is horrible about a trouble like this is that one cannot, as in any other — in loss, in death — bear one's trouble in peace; one must act," he said, as though guessing her thought. "One has to get out of the humiliating position one is in; one cannot live _à trois_."

"I understand, I quite understand that," Dolly said, and her head sank. She was silent for a moment, thinking of herself, of her own grief in her family, and then suddenly, with an impulsive movement, she raised her head and clasped her hands in an imploring gesture. "But wait — you are a Christian. Think of her! What will become of her if you cast her off?"

"I have thought, Darya Alexandrovna, I have thought a great deal," Alexey Alexandrovitch said. His face went red in patches, and his dim eyes stared straight ahead. Darya Alexandrovna at that moment pitied him with all her heart. "That is what I did, in fact, when she herself made my humiliation known to me; I left everything as it was. I gave her a chance to reform, I tried to save her. And what came of it? She wouldn't observe the slightest request — that she should keep up appearances," he said, growing heated. "One can save anyone who doesn't want to be ruined; but if her whole nature is so corrupt, so depraved, that ruin itself seems to her salvation — what is one to do?"
"Anything, only not a divorce!" answered Darya Alexandrovna.
"But what is anything?"
"No, it's awful! She'll be no one's wife, she'll be lost!"

"What can I do?" Alexey Alexandrovitch said, raising his shoulders and his eyebrows. The memory of his wife's last act had so enraged him that he turned frigid again, as he had been at the start of the conversation. "I am very grateful for your sympathy, but I must be going," he said, getting up.

"No, wait a minute. You must not ruin her. Wait a little; I'll tell you about myself. I was married, and my husband deceived me; in anger and jealousy I would have thrown up everything, I would myself.... But I came to my senses; and who did it? Anna saved me. And here I am, still living on. The children are growing up, my husband has come back to his family and feels his fault, is growing purer, better, and I live on.... I have forgiven it, and you ought to forgive too!"

Alexey Alexandrovitch heard her out, but her words had no effect on him now. All the hatred of the day he had decided on a divorce had risen up again in his soul. He shook himself and said in a shrill, loud voice:

"Forgive I cannot, and do not wish to, and I regard it as wrong. I have done everything for this woman, and she has trampled it all into the mud to which she is akin. I am not a spiteful man, I have never hated anyone, but I hate her with my whole soul, and I cannot even forgive her, because I hate her too much for all the wrong she has done me!" he said, with notes of hatred in his voice.
"Love those that hate you...." Darya Alexandrovna whispered timidly.
Alexey Alexandrovitch smiled contemptuously. He had known that long ago, but it could not be applied to his case.

"Love those that hate you — but to love those one hates is impossible. Forgive me for having troubled you. Everyone has enough to bear in his own grief!" And, recovering his self-possession, Alexey Alexandrovitch quietly took his leave and went away.
